mem.t: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

lessons.title: The Prodigal Comes Home
lessons.theme: The spiritual life begins not with effort, but with coming home

v: “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath and let it out slowly. Tell the Lord, “Lord, I’m home.” Take the busyness, the guilt and the burdens in your heart and lay them at the Father’s feet, the way a traveller sets down a heavy pack.
teach: Many people think of the spiritual life as a performance review: how many chapters I read, how long I prayed, how many times I slipped up. But the story of the prodigal son tells us that the first step of the spiritual life is not “doing better.” It is “turning around and coming home.”

Notice what the father does: he “saw,” he “was moved with compassion,” he “ran,” he “fell on his neck,” he “kissed him.” All five verbs belong to the father; every move is his. The son has not even finished his rehearsed confession before the father interrupts him and gives him a robe (honour), a ring (authority) and sandals (sonship, for slaves went barefoot).

This is the gospel: God does not wait for us to become good before he accepts us; he accepts us in order to make us good. Change your mindset and your life will change—from “I must work hard to make God love me” to “God already loves me, and I respond to his love.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The prodigal leaving home is the self-ruled life at its extreme—“Give me my share of the property”—wanting to be his own master. Coming home means stepping down from the throne of self and returning to his place as a son. Humility is the key to revival, and coming home is the first step of humility.
q: Who is God? — From the father’s five actions, what kind of God do you see?
Who am I? — Are you more like the prodigal leaving home, the prodigal on the road back, or the older brother who stayed home while his heart wandered far away?
How shall I respond? — In what one area today do you need to “turn around and come home”?
lessons.jesus: The Jesus who told this parable is himself the embodiment of the father’s heart that “ran.” He left his heavenly home and travelled into the far country to find us; on the cross he was stripped of his clothes so that we could be clothed in the best robe.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that while I was still far off, you saw me and ran to me. I will no longer try to earn your love with my performance; I confess that I need you. Today I have come home. Please be the Lord of my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write one sentence: “I have come home, because…”
Say something accepting and unconditional to a family member or friend
Before each task today, pray silently: “Father, I’m home.”
lessons.noon: “But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran” — Lord, right now I come back into your arms too.

lessons.title: Seeing Our Problem: Self-Rule
lessons.theme: The root of humanity’s fall is wanting to take God’s place

v: for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

lessons.still: Be still for a moment and ask the Holy Spirit to shine like a flashlight into your heart: “Lord, search me, and show me the places in me that are centred on myself.” Don’t rush, don’t defend yourself—just let him shine his light.
teach: The heart of the serpent’s temptation is one sentence: “You will be like God.” The problem was not simply eating a piece of fruit. It was that humanity wanted to leave its place as human, grasp God’s power, and decide for itself what is good and what is evil.

This is the self-ruled life: centred on myself, wanting to be my own master and king. Its outward expression is pride. Isaiah puts it even more plainly: “Everyone has turned to his own way.” The essence of sin is that “my way” replaces “God’s way.”

We see our problem not to condemn ourselves but to be healed. It is like going to the doctor: the right diagnosis comes first, then the right prescription. Today’s diagnosis reads: my root problem is not my circumstances, and not other people—it is the “self” inside me that wants to be king.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our place and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our place—let people be people and let God be God. The focus is not on other people’s faults, but on my own need for the Lord’s light.
q: Who is God? — When God sets boundaries for us, do they come from restriction or from love?
Who am I? — Where recently have you wanted to “decide good and evil” for yourself and be your own master?
How shall I respond? — Which piece of “my way” are you willing to hand back to God?
lessons.jesus: The first Adam said in the garden, “I will be like God.” Jesus, the last Adam, said in the garden of Gethsemane, “Not my will, but yours, be done.” Jesus is the perfect example of the self-emptied life.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often turn to my own way, wanting to be my own master and king. Thank you for laying my iniquity on yourself. Please tear down the pride in me, so that I can return to my place as a human being and let you be God. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down one thing where you recently “took charge” yourself, and entrust it to the Lord
When things don’t go your way today, first ask: “Who is on the throne right now?”
Say a humble word to someone you have treated with pride
lessons.noon: “All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way.” — Lord, right now I lay down my way and follow yours.

lessons.title: Seeing God’s Grace: The Cross
lessons.theme: God has prepared a complete solution for us

v: For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a good person someone would even dare to die.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God,
not of works, that no one would boast.

lessons.still: Picture yourself standing at the foot of the cross. You don’t need to say anything—just look up. Let that love, given “while we were yet sinners,” slowly fill your heart.
teach: Yesterday we saw the problem; today we see the answer. Paul uses three words to describe our condition: “weak,” “sinners,” and elsewhere, “enemies.” God’s love was not shown when we were most lovable, but when we were least lovable.

The cross dealt with two things: Jesus’ death dealt with both our sins and our sinful nature; Jesus’ resurrection gives us new life. We are not saved by patching up the old life, but by receiving a completely new one.

“By grace… through faith”—grace is the gift on God’s side; faith is the empty hand we hold out on ours. If a gift had to be earned by works, it would no longer be a gift, and people would boast. The gospel takes away every reason to boast and leaves only thanksgiving.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Everything is what God has done and accomplished in Jesus; all of it is God’s grace. So the glory does not go to me but to Jesus. Only through the truth of the gospel can we live the self-emptied life.
q: Who is God? — How does the phrase “while we were yet sinners” help you know God’s love?
Who am I? — Are you still quietly trying to “earn” God’s acceptance with good works?
How shall I respond? — How will you express your thanks today?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished!” He left no work for us to complete. Our spiritual practice is not finishing our salvation, but resting and responding within a salvation that is already complete.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for dying for me while I was still a sinner. I lay down my own merits and hold out empty hands to receive your grace. From today on, my whole life will be a response of thanksgiving. All glory to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three things about the cross that you will thank God for today
Memorise Ephesians 2:8 and repeat it silently three times
Make “Glory to the Lord” your silent prayer as you finish each small task today
lessons.noon: “In that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Lord, right now I look to your grace alone.

lessons.title: A New Creation
lessons.theme: It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me

v: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

lessons.still: Place your hand on your chest and say quietly, “Lord Jesus, you live in me.” Sense his presence—not far away in heaven, but near, in your heart. The Holy Spirit dwells in the heart, not in the head.
teach: A caterpillar does not become a butterfly by working hard at “learning to fly.” It goes through death and new birth inside the chrysalis; its very nature changes, and then it flies naturally. It is the same for Christians: we are not “old selves trying hard to be good,” but “new creations.”

Galatians 2:20 is the manifesto of the self-emptied life: the self-ruled life of the old self has been “crucified with Christ”; the self-emptied life of the new self is “Christ lives in me.” Self-emptying does not mean becoming nothing; it means letting the infinite Christ live out his infinite life in me.

Then why do we still fail? Because we often forget who we are and slip back into the habits of the old self. So our daily practice is to change our mindset again and again: I am already a new creation; today I choose to let Christ live in me.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life lets Jesus live within; only the self-emptied life lets Jesus reign; only the self-emptied life can be led by the Holy Spirit. The self-ruled life of the old self becoming the self-emptied life of the new self—this is how a defeated life becomes an overcoming life.
q: Who is God? — “Who loved me, and gave himself up for me”: how have you experienced this personal love?
Who am I? — In what area are you still living like the “old self”?
How shall I respond? — In what situation today will you let Christ live in you?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him.” He lived in complete dependence on the Father. Today this same Jesus lives in me, and his life is my overcoming life.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for making me a new creation. The old has passed away; I am no longer defined by my past. Today it is not I who live, but you who live in me. Please reign in my words, my thoughts and my reactions. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: When you face a challenge today, say silently: “No longer I, but Christ.”
Write down one habit of the old self and how the new self would respond instead
Memorise this week’s verse: 2 Corinthians 5:17
lessons.noon: “And it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” — Lord, right now please live in me.

lessons.title: Let Jesus Reign
lessons.theme: Denying ourselves to follow the Lord is the freest road of all

v: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.
For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it.
Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.

lessons.still: Quietly spread out today’s plans before the Lord one by one, like handing over keys to their owner one at a time. Say, “Lord, these are all yours.”
teach: This week we have walked a road: coming home (Day 1) → seeing our self-rule (Day 2) → seeing grace (Day 3) → becoming a new self (Day 4) → and today, letting Jesus reign.

When Jesus speaks of denying ourselves, there are three actions: deny yourself, take up your cross daily, and follow. Notice the word “daily.” Letting Jesus reign is not a one-time decision but a choice we make every morning. A ship can only have one captain; if I don’t step down, the Lord cannot take the helm.

Philippians shows us the heart of Jesus: he existed in the form of God, yet “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.” Instead he emptied himself, humbled himself and obeyed. The first Adam grasped at power, wanting to become God; Jesus laid down power and became human. This is humility: laying down power and returning to our place.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The two core values—let Jesus reign; let Jesus receive all the glory. Denying ourselves means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. Humility inspires humility and brings a win for everyone; this is where building what belongs to God begins.
q: Who is God? — What kind of God do you see in the way Jesus “emptied himself”?
Who am I? — Which room of your life does the Lord not yet rule (time, money, relationships, dreams)?
How shall I respond? — Which “key” will you hand to the Lord today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the living model of self-denial: he gave up the glory of heaven, gave up his own will, and gave up his own life. He does not merely tell us to walk this road; he walked it ahead of us, and now he lives in us and walks it with us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I am willing to deny myself, take up my cross daily and follow you. I give up the throne of my life to you. Please reign over my time, my money, my relationships and my dreams. May you receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Make a list of “the rooms of my life” and hand each one over to the Lord
Do something small for someone else, not for yourself, and don’t let anyone know
Tomorrow (Saturday), share the grace of this week with a spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself.” — Lord, right now I let you reign.

mem.t: “Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted on the earth.”

lessons.title: Be Still and Know
lessons.theme: Stillness is not emptiness; it is knowing that God is God

v: “Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted on the earth.”
The LORD of Armies is with us. The God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah.
My soul rests in God alone. My salvation is from him.
He alone is my rock, my salvation, and my fortress. I will never be greatly shaken.

lessons.still: Find a corner where you won’t be disturbed. Turn off notifications and lay your phone face down. Plant both feet on the floor and breathe slowly three times. Don’t hurry to speak; simply repeat in your heart, “You are God, and I am not.” Let those words sink slowly to the bottom of your heart.
teach: Stir a glass of muddy water and the more you stir, the cloudier it gets; but set it on the table and leave it alone, and the silt settles to the bottom and the water clears. Our hearts are the same. When we keep scrolling, rushing from one appointment to the next and scheming solutions, our hearts grow cloudy, and we can see neither God nor ourselves clearly. Being still means letting the water in the glass of our heart come to rest.

Psalm 46 was written in a world where mountains shake and seas roar. Into that upheaval God says, “Be still”—words that carry the sense of “let go, stop”: unclench your fists. Then he says, “Know that I am God.” Stillness is not escaping from reality; it is affirming afresh, right in the middle of reality, that God is in control—not me, and not my circumstances.

So stillness begins with a change of mindset: from “I must control everything” to “God is in control, so I can stop.” This is the posture of faith. David says, “My soul rests in God alone.” Silence here does not mean nothing is happening; it means handing the initiative back to God and waiting for him to speak first and act first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When we cannot be still, self-rule is often at work—we fear things will spin out of control, so we cling tightly to power. Stillness is laying down power and returning to our place: let people be people and let God be God. When our focus turns from our circumstances back to Jesus, our hearts find rest.
q: Who is God? — In the “shaking mountains and roaring seas” of your life, what comfort do the words “I am God” bring you?
Who am I? — What is hardest for you to let go of—what do you most want to hold on to tightly?
How shall I respond? — At what time today will you deliberately stop for five minutes?
lessons.jesus: In the storm the disciples panicked, but Jesus was asleep on a cushion in the stern. He got up and rebuked the wind: “Peace! Be still!” Jesus’ calm was not ignorance of the danger; it was complete trust in the Father. The Lord who stilled the storm wants to still our hearts too.
lessons.pray: Almighty God, you are my refuge and my strength. I confess that I am often bound by busyness and worry, wanting to control everything myself. Today I unclench my hands and become still before you, acknowledging that you are God and I am not. Make my heart like settled water, so that I can see you clearly. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Find five minutes today, turn off your phone, and quietly meditate on Psalm 46:10
Write down one thing you can’t let go of, and beside it write: “You are God”
Before replying to messages today, pause and take one deep breath
lessons.noon: “Be still, and know that I am God.” — Lord, right now I let go and let you be God.

lessons.title: Martha and Mary
lessons.theme: Only one thing is needed: sitting at Jesus’ feet

v: She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.still: Imagine walking into that little house in Bethany. The kitchen is still smoking and the work isn’t finished. Today, don’t go into the kitchen first; go and sit down at Jesus’ feet. Rest your hands on your knees and say to the Lord, “I’m here. Please speak.”
teach: When our phone battery drops to five percent, we hurry to find a charger; but when our spiritual battery runs empty, we often just keep pushing on. That was Martha. She loved the Lord and was busy preparing for him, but the busier she got, the more frazzled she became, until she even complained to the Lord: “Don’t you care?”

Jesus calls her name twice—“Martha, Martha”—a tender call, not a rebuke. He points out that the problem is not “much serving” but being “anxious and troubled”: a heart pulled apart and divided by many things. “One thing is needed”: being with the Lord first. What Mary chose was not laziness but the right order.

The order of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, then with tasks. Martha put tasks ahead of the Lord, so her serving became a burden; Mary first received at the Lord’s feet, so her serving afterwards became an overflow. The cure for frantic busyness is not doing nothing, but sitting down first and then getting up.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Being busy for the Lord while forgetting the Lord is self-rule dressed up as service; sitting at the Lord’s feet is letting Jesus reign, and it puts our service back in the right order.
q: Who is God? — When Jesus says, “Martha, Martha,” what does his tone show you about his heart?
Who am I? — What are the “many things” that have recently made you “anxious and troubled”?
How shall I respond? — Tomorrow morning, how will you sit at the Lord’s feet first before starting your work?
lessons.jesus: In his own busiest seasons, Jesus often withdrew to the wilderness to pray. He was never driven by the crowd’s demands; he received his next step from his fellowship with the Father. His service was never frantic, because his heart was always at rest in the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I am often like Martha, anxious and troubled about many things, even complaining that you don’t care. Please call my name tenderly, help me to stop, and let me sit at your feet. I choose the good part: to be with you first, and then go and do what you have entrusted to me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: List today’s to-do items, and add at the very top: “Be with the Lord first”
As you do housework or your job today, speak a sentence to the Lord while you work
Drop one unnecessary busyness and give that time to the Lord or your family
lessons.noon: “But one thing is needed.” — Lord, right now I lay down my busyness and return to your feet.

lessons.title: Speak, Your Servant Is Listening
lessons.theme: The purpose of stillness is hearing God’s voice

v: The LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” Then Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.”
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.

lessons.still: Sit quietly and rest your open hands on your knees, as if ready to receive a gift. Say softly, “Lord, speak; your servant is listening.” Then stay silent for two minutes. Don’t rush to fill the space—just wait.
teach: A radio has to be tuned to the right frequency to pick up a clear programme; drift slightly off and all you get is static. God is always speaking, but our hearts are often crowded with other voices—work, social media, the noise inside ourselves. Being still means tuning our hearts back to God’s frequency.

Three times the boy Samuel heard someone calling, and each time he thought it was Eli. He did not yet know God’s voice and needed a spiritual elder to teach him how to respond: “Speak; for your servant hears.” Notice the order: not “Your servant speaks, Lord, please listen,” but “Lord, please speak; your servant listens.” Jesus also said, “My sheep hear my voice.” Listening is the sheep’s duty—and the sheep’s blessing.

God speaks to us mainly through Scripture. The Holy Spirit may also prompt us in prayer, or confirm something through a spiritual companion. The test for discernment is clear: God’s voice never contradicts Scripture; it always points to Jesus; and it brings repentance and peace, not accusation and confusion. Once we have heard, the best response is to obey.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide. Listen with the heart, rather than calculating with the head; first say “Speak,” then say “I’m willing.” A willingness to listen is where the self-emptied life begins—no longer “I have the final say,” but “the Lord has the final say.”
q: Who is God? — God called Samuel three times; what does this show you about how patiently he seeks people out?
Who am I? — Are your prayers more often “Your servant speaks” or “Your servant listens”?
How shall I respond? — In today’s reading, which sentence do you sense the Lord is speaking to you?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” His whole life was spent listening to the Father and obeying him. He not only teaches us to listen; he modelled listening for us. And now, as the Good Shepherd, he calls his own sheep himself.
lessons.pray: Jesus, Good Shepherd, thank you for calling my name yourself. My heart is often so crowded with voices that I can’t hear your word clearly. Today I become still and say to you: Speak, your servant is listening. Holy Spirit, open my ears, so that when I hear, I will be willing to follow. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: When you pray today, spend two minutes not speaking, only listening
Save one sentence from today’s reading that moved you in your phone’s notes
Ask a spiritual elder: How do you discern God’s leading?
lessons.noon: “My sheep hear my voice.” — Lord, right now speak; your servant is listening.

lessons.title: From the Heart, Not the Head
lessons.theme: Guard your heart, and let God’s peace stand watch at its door

v: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Place your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat. Tell the Lord, “I hand over to you the thoughts that keep spinning in my head.” Each time a worry comes to mind, say gently, “I give this to you,” until your heart slowly grows calm.
teach: On a sleepless night, the mind is like a washing machine that won’t stop, churning the same thing over and over: What if…? What if…? The more we think, the more awake and troubled we become. This is how “living from the head brings worry”: we try to calculate everything with our own minds, and all we come up with is anxiety.

Proverbs says that out of the heart “is the wellspring of life.” In the Bible the “heart” is the core of a person, the seat of trust and love. Paul’s prescription is not “stop thinking” but a transfer: in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, tell God. The result is that God’s peace will “guard” our hearts and thoughts—a word that originally meant soldiers on sentry duty. Peace stands like a guard at the door of the heart.

Living from the heart does not mean abandoning reason; it means putting the mind back in its proper place—no longer sitting on the throne, but serving under the Holy Spirit’s leading. Here is the key change of mindset: from “I’ll have peace once I figure it out” to “I have peace once I entrust it.” Living from the heart brings joy, because the heart is open to the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself. The Holy Spirit dwells in the heart, not in the head. Living from the head is taking charge and trying to solve everything myself; living from the heart is letting Jesus reign and receiving, in trust, the peace that surpasses all understanding.
q: Who is God? — What does “peace… which surpasses all understanding” tell you about how God’s peace differs from the world’s?
Who am I? — When are you most likely to find that “living from the head brings worry”?
How shall I respond? — Which worry today will you hand to God through “prayer with thanksgiving”?
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus said to his disciples, “Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me.” Facing the cross, he still left his peace with his disciples. His heart rested completely in the Father, and today he gives that same peace to us.
lessons.pray: Lord, my mind is often crammed with worries as I try to calculate tomorrow on my own. Today I hand these thoughts over to you one by one, and I thank you for your faithfulness in the past. May your peace stand guard over my heart like a sentry, so that I live from the heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, and no longer from the head, relying on myself. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three worries, and beside each one write a sentence of thanks
When anxiety rises, say silently: “In nothing be anxious—just pray”
Before bed, hand tomorrow over to the Lord, and then close your eyes
lessons.noon: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer.” — Lord, right now I give my worries to you.

lessons.title: Carrying Stillness into Daily Life
lessons.theme: Stillness is not just a time slot but a state of heart

v: For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” You refused,
Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.

lessons.still: Think through the rest of today’s schedule. At each transition point—leaving home, going into a meeting, coming back home—picture yourself pausing for one second to look up to the Lord. Then say quietly, “Lord, I’m taking you with me into today.”
teach: When a typhoon is at its fiercest, its eye is perfectly calm. Christian stillness is not running off to live as a hermit on a mountain; it is having an eye in the storm of life—the place where the Lord is present. However busy things are outside, inside we can still be at rest.

When Israel faced a crisis, they wanted to rely on Egypt’s horses, but God said, “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” Sadly, “You refused.” Jesus is the opposite example: while it was still dark, he went out to a deserted place to pray. Because he had quiet in the early morning, he could move through the crowds all day without being hurried.

This week we have learned that stillness is knowing that God is God, coming back from busyness to the Lord’s feet, listening for the Lord’s voice, and living from the heart rather than the head. Today we carry it into everyday life: a regular time of stillness each morning, plus many brief moments of “looking up” throughout the day. Next week we will open the Bible in that stillness and learn to meet God there.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Our focus is on Jesus—not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. Everyday stillness means turning our focus back to Jesus again and again; when we let Jesus reign at every transition point, our lives gradually become part of what belongs to God.
q: Who is God? — “Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence”: how is God’s strength different from human effort?
Who am I? — Have you “refused” to be still, preferring to rely on your own “horses of Egypt”?
How shall I respond? — What regular morning time of stillness will you set for yourself?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was surrounded by crowds and chased by needs, yet he was never flustered. Before dawn he went to the wilderness to commune with the Father, and he often took his disciples to quiet places to rest a while. His day began in stillness, so even amid the clamour he could stay focused on the Father’s will.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for teaching me to be still this week. I confess that I often refuse to rest and would rather rush about relying on myself. Help me to come before you first thing each morning, and to look up to you often in the busyness of the day. In every storm, may my heart know the rest of your presence. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Set a regular time and place for stillness tomorrow morning, and set an alarm
Each time you walk through a door or get into a car today, pray silently: “The Lord is with me”
Share with a spiritual companion one change that stillness has brought you this week
lessons.noon: “Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” — Lord, right now, in my busyness, I return to your rest.

mem.t: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

lessons.title: The Word God Breathed Out
lessons.theme: Scripture is God’s word, the standard for life

v: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,
that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.
For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.

lessons.still: Hold your Bible in both hands and be still for a moment. Tell the Lord, “This is your word, not human opinion.” Ask the Holy Spirit to help you open this book today with reverence and longing.
teach: If a map were drawn by someone who had never been to the place, we would not dare to trust it on a mountain trail. But if it were drawn by the very one who made the mountains, we could follow it with confidence. The Bible is that kind of map: not human guesses about God, but God’s revelation to humanity.

The word “inspired” literally means “God-breathed.” Just as God breathed into Adam and he became a living being, God moved people by his Spirit to write the Scriptures, and so this book carries God’s own breath. Peter says prophecy never came from the will of man; rather, people spoke from God as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. That is why Scripture is profitable for us in four ways: teaching, reproof, correction and instruction in righteousness.

Our mindset shapes how we read the Bible. If we treat it as a reference book, we will read only the parts we like; if we treat it as God’s word, we will let it examine us. The purpose of reading Scripture is not to make us people with lots of knowledge, but “that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: One of the three foundations—Scripture is my standard. It is not I who judge Scripture, but Scripture that judges me. Laying down my own opinions and returning to my place as a learner is letting Jesus reign in the realm of truth.
q: Who is God? — What kind of God is willing to “speak” and to put his heart into writing?
Who am I? — Do you more often let Scripture “examine you,” or do you “pick and choose” from Scripture?
How shall I respond? — How will you show today that Scripture has the final authority in your life?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted, three times he answered, “It is written.” He was the Son of God, yet he gladly took Scripture as his standard; he also said, “The Scripture can’t be broken.” If the Lord himself honoured Scripture this way, how much more should we take it as the standard for our lives.
lessons.pray: God who speaks, thank you that you did not leave us groping in the dark, but wrote your heart down for us in the Scriptures. Give me a reverent heart to receive your word without picking and choosing and without watering it down. Holy Spirit, use your word to teach me, reprove me and correct me, so that I may be complete. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: On the inside cover of your Bible, write: “This is God’s word, my standard”
Before reading Scripture today, pray: “Lord, please speak to me through your word”
Memorise 2 Timothy 3:16
lessons.noon: “Every Scripture is God-breathed.” — Lord, right now I am willing to be shaped by your word.

lessons.title: Read, Reflect, Pray, Do
lessons.theme: Four steps that bring God’s word into our lives

v: This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.
but his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.

lessons.still: Choose the short passage you will read today, but don’t rush into it. Take a deep breath and tell the Lord, “I haven’t come to finish my homework; I’ve come to meet you.” Then read it slowly the first time, as you would read a letter from home sent from far away.
teach: You can’t eat a meal by just reading the menu, nor by bolting it down whole. You put it in your mouth, chew it slowly, swallow and digest it, and finally it becomes strength for your work. Reading Scripture is the same: reading is putting it in your mouth, reflecting is chewing, praying is digesting and absorbing, and doing is turning it into strength. Skip any step and you lose part of the nourishment.

Joshua 1:8 itself contains clear steps: “shall not depart from your mouth”—read; “meditate on it day and night”—reflect; “observe to do”—do. Psalm 1 says such a person is like a tree planted by streams of water. The word “meditate” originally carries the sense of murmuring something over and over in a low voice—like a cow chewing the cud, turning the word over and over until it becomes your prayer.

In practice: Read—read a short passage slowly and circle the words that touch you. Reflect—ask, “What does this passage show me about God? About myself?” Pray—turn that sentence into a prayer, responding to God. Do—set one concrete small action for today. This is exactly the daily flow of this app.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Changing our mindset takes eight steps, from Information and Revelation to Conviction and Practice. The four steps of Bible reading walk this very road: reading is Information, reflecting seeks Revelation, praying is Conviction, and doing is Practice. A changed mindset changes our life, and a changed life changes how we live.
q: Who is God? — God promises “good success”; what kind of relationship is that promise built on?
Who am I? — Of the four steps—read, reflect, pray, do—which do you most often skip?
How shall I respond? — Which passage will you read today using the four steps?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ life was a life saturated with Scripture. Tempted in the wilderness, he quoted Deuteronomy readily; on the cross he still prayed the Psalms. God’s word was not only on his lips but in his heart and in his actions. He is the one who read, reflected, prayed and did most perfectly.
lessons.pray: Lord, I don’t want to just look at the menu and never eat the bread of life. Teach me to meditate on your word day and night, letting it pass from my mouth into my heart, become my prayer, and then turn into my actions. Make me like a tree planted by streams of water, bearing fruit in its season. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read Psalm 1 using the four steps, and write down one action for today
Say a verse that touched you today three times, like chewing the cud
Rewrite a verse as your own prayer
lessons.noon: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night.” — Lord, right now I chew on your word again.

lessons.title: Meeting the Lord in Scripture
lessons.theme: We read Scripture to come to Jesus and receive life

v: “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me.
Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.
They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”

lessons.still: Imagine you are one of the disciples on the road to Emmaus, walking along in disappointment and confusion, when a stranger comes alongside you. Say quietly, “Lord, please open the Scriptures to me yourself today, and set my heart on fire.”
teach: If someone read every biography of a famous person but never met or spoke with them, they would only “know about” that person; they would not truly “know” them. Bible reading can be like that: more and more knowledge, but a heart growing colder and colder—even turning proud and using verses to measure others.

Jesus said to religious leaders who knew the Scriptures well: You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life, yet they testify about me, and you will not come to me to have life. The problem was not that they hadn’t read enough, but that after reading they would not “come.” The disciples on the road to Emmaus were the opposite: as the Lord opened the Scriptures to them, their hearts burned within them.

So as we read, we should keep asking, “What kind of Jesus does this passage show me?” The Bible is like a road, and its destination is Jesus himself. Our mindset needs to shift from “How many chapters must I finish?” to “Whom will I meet today?” The amount is not the point; the meeting is.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example; Scripture is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide—and all three meet in Bible reading: the Holy Spirit opens the Scriptures so that I see Jesus. Knowledge that puffs us up becomes mere decoration for the self-ruled life; a real encounter makes us humble and on fire.
q: Who is God? — Jesus drew near to his discouraged disciples; what does this show you about his heart?
Who am I? — When you read the Bible, is your heart more cold or on fire? Why?
How shall I respond? — After reading today, with what words will you respond to the Lord you have met?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus walked a long road with two discouraged disciples, and beginning from Moses and all the prophets he explained to them what the Scriptures said about himself. The whole Bible is his self-introduction. Even now, by the Holy Spirit, he opens our minds so that we meet him in the Scriptures.
lessons.pray: Risen Lord, I don’t want merely to know things about you without knowing you. As you did on the road to Emmaus, open the Scriptures to me yourself, open my mind, and set my heart on fire. Every time I open the Bible, let me come to you and receive life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: After reading today, write: “The Jesus I saw today is…”
Let go of the pressure of a reading plan; read just a short passage and chew on it slowly
Share with a friend a verse that set your heart on fire
lessons.noon: “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way?” — Lord, right now please speak to me again.

lessons.title: After Looking in the Mirror
lessons.theme: Hearing and doing the word builds our life on the rock

v: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock.

lessons.still: Recall a verse you read yesterday and quietly ask yourself, “Did I do it?” Don’t rush to defend yourself or to blame yourself; simply see it honestly before the Lord, and then say, “Lord, today I am willing to do it.”
teach: Imagine looking in the mirror in the morning, seeing a smudge on your face, then turning away, forgetting all about it, and going out with the smudge all day. It sounds absurd. Yet James says that is exactly what people are like who hear the word and don’t do it: they see themselves in the mirror of Scripture, yet nothing changes.

James calls this “deluding your own selves”—thinking that knowing is the same as doing. Jesus told of two men building houses. Both heard his words, and on an ordinary day their houses looked much the same; the difference only showed when the storm came. One “does them,” and his house is built on the rock; the other does not, and his house is built on sand.

Obedience is not gritting our teeth with willpower; it is the obedience that responds to grace. Start small: each time you read, set just one action you can do today; in the evening review it, reflect and correct, then repeat the next day. Truth only truly becomes ours when we live it out.
lessons.light: 321 Light: In the eight steps of changing our mindset, Conviction is followed by Practice, Review, Correction and Repetition. Knowing without doing stops at “Information”; when we live it out, our mindset becomes life, and life becomes the way we live. Letting Jesus reign means letting his word have the final say in me.
q: Who is God? — When God gives us the mirror of Scripture, is it to condemn us or to heal us?
Who am I? — Which truth have you long “known” but still not put into practice?
How shall I respond? — Which word you already know will you put into practice right away today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work.” For him, obeying the Father’s word was not a burden but nourishment. From the manger to the cross, his whole life was God’s word put into practice.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often hear and then forget; I know a great deal but do very little. Forgive me for deceiving myself. Today I want to build my life on the rock of your word—not only hearing it, but doing it. Holy Spirit, give me the strength to obey. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Choose a verse you have long known but not yet practised, and live it out today
In the evening, take three minutes to review: Did I do what I read today?
Tell a spiritual companion about today’s practice and ask them to check in with you
lessons.noon: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man.” — Lord, right now I am willing to obey.

lessons.title: A Lamp to My Feet
lessons.theme: God’s word lights up today’s next step

v: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
The entrance of your words gives light. It gives understanding to the simple.

lessons.still: Imagine walking a mountain path at night with only a small lamp in your hand, lighting up just a step or two ahead. Quietly tell the Lord, “I don’t need to see the whole journey; I only ask you to light up my next step today.”
teach: The oil lamps of ancient times were not very bright; they lit only a short stretch of path just ahead. The psalmist says God’s word is “a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path”—not a floodlight on the blueprint of the next ten years, but light for how to walk today. We often want to see the whole route clearly before we set out, but God invites us to follow the light one step at a time.

“The entrance of your words gives light. It gives understanding to the simple.” The light does not come from our cleverness but from God’s word being opened up—like drawing back the curtains so the light pours in. So we read Scripture with a humble heart, admitting that we are “the simple” who need light. The proud, who think they see clearly, end up seeing nothing.

This week we have seen that Scripture is the God-breathed standard; that we read it through four steps—read, reflect, pray, do; that the purpose of reading is to meet Jesus; and that obeying matters more than knowing. Today we hide God’s word in our hearts and let it shine at every fork in the road. Next week we will learn to respond to this speaking God through the Lord’s Prayer, which Jesus himself taught.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard. Our perspective shifts—from the human point of view to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal. Letting God’s word be a lamp to our feet means letting Jesus reign in every choice, building what belongs to God step by step.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to lead us “step by step”; what does this show you about his patience?
Who am I? — Do you often hesitate to take the next step because you can’t see the whole road?
How shall I respond? — Which choice you face today needs the light of God’s word?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” God’s word is a lamp because it points to the true Light. Those who follow Jesus don’t need to see the whole road first; they only need to follow the light closely.
lessons.pray: Lord, your word is a lamp to my feet and a light for my path. I don’t ask to see the whole road; I only ask you to light up my next step today. Open up your words and give understanding to someone as simple as me; and help me to hide your word in my heart and follow you at every fork in the road. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Memorise this week’s verse: Psalm 119:105
Write down a decision you are facing, and find a related verse
At the weekend, share with a spiritual companion one ray of light you received from Scripture this week
lessons.noon: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” — Lord, right now please light up my next step.

mem.t: Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

lessons.title: Our Father in Heaven
lessons.theme: Prayer begins with knowing the Father and coming to him

v: Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need before you ask him.
Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”

lessons.still: Become still and call softly, “Abba, Father.” Repeat it a few times, letting those words settle slowly into your heart. Picture yourself walking into your father’s room like a child—no appointment needed, no speech to prepare.
teach: When children ask their dad for something, they never prepare an eloquent speech first; they simply call out, “Dad!” Many people are afraid to pray because they imagine prayer as addressing a distant authority: the words must be beautiful and it must go on long enough. In teaching us to pray, Jesus tears down that misunderstanding with the very first line.

Jesus says not to pile up empty repetitions like the pagans, because “your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.” Prayer is not informing God of something he doesn’t know; it is fellowship between children and their Father. “Our Father in heaven”—“our” reminds us we never pray alone; “in heaven” reminds us he is Most High; “Father” reminds us he is nearest and dearest.

Paul says that we did not receive a spirit of slavery but the Spirit of adoption as sons, so we cry, “Abba! Father!” This is the cry the Holy Spirit raises within us. Our mindset must change: I do not earn the right to be a child by praying; I can pray because I am already a child.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships—God comes first. Prayer is first of all a relationship, not a tool. The heart of a slave is the self-ruled life, trading performance for rewards; the heart of a son is the self-emptied life, resting in the Father’s love. The Lord’s Prayer is the blueprint for building what belongs to God, and it all begins with “Father.”
q: Who is God? — How does “your Father knows” change the way you see prayer?
Who am I? — When you pray, are you more like a servant giving a report or a child talking to their father?
How shall I respond? — How will you speak to the Father like a child today?
lessons.jesus: In his most agonising hour in Gethsemane, Jesus still cried, “Abba, Father.” He is God’s only Son, with an eternal, intimate relationship with the Father; through the cross he shares that relationship with us, so that we too can call God Father.
lessons.pray: Abba, heavenly Father, thank you that I am no longer a slave but your child. I don’t need beautiful words; you already know what I need. Today I come before you like a child, open my heart to you, and rest in your love. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: As you pray today, begin with “Abba, Father” and simply say three things that are on your heart
Write down one way the heavenly Father has cared for you, and thank him specifically
When praying for a friend, say “our Father,” remembering that you are family
lessons.noon: “For your Father knows what things you need before you ask him.” — Lord, my Father, right now I rest and rely on you.

lessons.title: May Your Name Be Kept Holy
lessons.theme: Prayer cares first about God’s name, not mine

v: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.
Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew.
One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”

lessons.still: Close your eyes and picture the throne and the seraphim Isaiah saw. Today, don’t rush to ask for anything; just say softly three times, “Holy, holy, holy.” Let God’s greatness fill your heart first, and then begin to pray.
teach: A telescope brings a distant planet near and magnifies it. It doesn’t actually make the planet bigger; it lets us see how big it really is. “Hallowing God’s name” is like that: we cannot make God any holier, but we can “magnify” his holiness in our lives so that others see the greatness he truly has.

Isaiah saw the Lord in the year King Uzziah died—the earthly throne stood empty, but the Lord still sat on the heavenly throne. The seraphim covered their faces and feet with their wings and cried, “Holy!” “Holy” means set apart, transcendent, and perfectly pure. The first petition of the Lord’s Prayer is not for ourselves but for God’s name.

Our prayers often look like a shopping list centred on “me.” Jesus reverses the order: first God’s name, God’s kingdom and God’s will, and only then our needs. This doesn’t mean our needs are unimportant; rather, when God is put first, everything else finds its proper place.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One of the two core values—let Jesus receive all the glory. “Hallowing his name” means not stealing God’s glory. Self-ruled people are like the builders of Babel, wanting to “make a name for ourselves”; self-emptied people want only God’s name to be lifted high.
q: Who is God? — The seraphim cover their faces and cry “Holy”; what does this show you of God’s majesty?
Who am I? — In your prayers, how much is for God’s name and how much for your own needs?
How shall I respond? — In what situation today could you lead people to honour God because of you?
lessons.jesus: In his prayer before he was betrayed, Jesus said, “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” The goal of his whole life was to glorify the Father’s name. He also prayed for us, that we would likewise make the Father’s name known in the world.
lessons.pray: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Armies! The whole earth is full of your glory. I confess that my prayers are often centred on myself. Today, first of all, I ask that your name be kept holy and lifted high in my words, my work and my family. May all glory go to you, not to me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: For the first three minutes of your prayer today, only praise God—make no requests
Before each task, pray silently: “May your name be kept holy here”
Turn something you were praised for into a testimony of God’s grace
lessons.noon: “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies!” — Lord, right now may your name be kept holy in me.

lessons.title: Let Your Kingdom Come
lessons.theme: Letting God reign is the most fundamental prayer

v: Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.”

lessons.still: Hold in your heart the one thing you care about most today. Quietly lift it before the Lord and say, “Lord, in this matter, let your kingdom come and let your will be done.” Then slowly open your hands.
teach: You can tell a nation’s territory by where its flag is planted. God’s kingdom is not a geographical territory but wherever God reigns as King. When I pray, “Let your Kingdom come,” I am saying, “Lord, plant your flag in my home, my work and my heart.”

“Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven”—just as the angels in heaven obey immediately, joyfully and completely, may it be so on earth. The truest demonstration of this line is in Gethsemane: sorrowful almost to death, Jesus still said, “Not what I desire, but what you desire.” God’s kingdom often comes when “what I desire” steps down from the throne.

This is this week’s memory verse and the heart of the Lord’s Prayer. It contains an exchange: laying down my kingdom and welcoming God’s. At first it may feel like a loss, but God’s will is always good, perfect and pleasing. Letting God reign is not a loss but a return to the very best plan.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The two core values—let Jesus reign; let Jesus receive all the glory. Building what belongs to God means fulfilling the Lord’s Prayer: his will done on earth as it is in heaven. Every time we say “not what I desire,” we lay one more brick in God’s kingdom system.
q: Who is God? — What does it mean for your life that God’s will is perfectly done in heaven?
Who am I? — In what matter is your prayer really “Let my kingdom come”?
How shall I respond? — In which decision today will you say, “What you desire”?
lessons.jesus: The first words of Jesus’ preaching were, “Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.” Wherever he went, the sick were healed, demons were driven out and sins were forgiven—God’s kingdom came in him. In Gethsemane he surrendered his will entirely to the Father, and the cross became the road to the kingdom’s victory.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, let your kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. I place my home, my work and my plans before you. Not what I desire, but what you desire. Reign in every corner of my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Memorise this week’s verse: Matthew 6:10
Before making a decision, pray first: “What you desire”
At home or at work, find one matter where you deliberately put God’s heart first
lessons.noon: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth.” — Lord, right now please reign here.

lessons.title: Today’s Bread and Forgiveness
lessons.theme: Relying on God’s provision daily, and living out forgiveness daily

v: Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

lessons.still: Quietly thank the Lord for what you need today: food, strength, wisdom. Then ask the Holy Spirit to bring a name to mind—someone you still can’t let go of. You don’t need to resolve it right away; simply bring that person honestly before the Lord.
teach: In the wilderness the Israelites gathered manna every morning, only enough for that day; if they kept extra until the next day, it bred worms and stank. God was training them to depend on him day by day. “Give us today our daily bread” is likewise an invitation to live a life of trust one day at a time, not carrying tomorrow’s worries into today.

Right after it comes, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Of all the lines in the Lord’s Prayer, this is the only one Jesus went on to explain. This does not mean forgiving others is the price of salvation; it means that those who have truly received great forgiveness will inevitably let forgiveness flow out. Refusing to forgive shows that the door of the heart has closed to grace as well.

It is no accident that bread and forgiveness sit side by side: the body needs daily bread, and relationships need daily forgiveness. Unforgiveness is like drinking poison yourself and waiting for the other person to collapse. Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened, nor is it instantly restoring trust; it is handing the right to judge back to God, and no longer letting bitterness reign in our hearts.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships—first with God, then with ourselves, then with others. Only when we receive forgiveness from God do we have the strength to forgive others. Pride says, “I have the right to hold a grudge”; humility lays down that power and lets God be the Judge. People matter more than things; don’t hurt people for the sake of things.
q: Who is God? — God provides every day and forgives every day; what does this show you of his abundance?
Who am I? — Are you still clutching some “debt” that someone owes you?
How shall I respond? — Whose name will you hand over to God today, to begin the journey of forgiveness?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the bread of life.” He doesn’t just provide food; he himself is the bread of life. On the cross he prayed for those who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” With his own body he accomplished the provision and the forgiveness we need.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for providing for my needs every day. Give me today my daily bread, and teach me to rely on you one day at a time. Thank you, too, for forgiving my enormous debt. Help me to forgive those who have hurt me, to hand judgement over to you, and not to let bitterness reign in my heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before each meal, thank God specifically for one provision
Write down a name you need to forgive, and pray one sentence of blessing over that person
Today, stop bringing up one way someone wronged you in the past
lessons.noon: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” — Lord, right now I hand judgement over to you.

lessons.title: Yours Is the Kingdom, the Power and the Glory
lessons.theme: Prayer begins with worship and ends with worship

v: Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’

Yours, LORD, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and on the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.

lessons.still: Quietly recall what you have prayed about this week. Then open your hands, palms upward, and declare, “Yours is the kingdom, the power and the glory.” Let these words seal all your requests like a stamp.
teach: The signature at the end of a letter determines the weight of the whole letter. The Lord’s Prayer closes with “yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory,” which is like stamping a seal on every request: all of this belongs to God and is accomplished by God. This ending keeps prayer centred on God from beginning to end.

“Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one”—we admit that we are weak and need God’s protection. Then the prayer turns to praise. After David gathered offerings to prepare for building the temple, he praised God in the same way: “Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty!” The people had given much, yet they confessed that everything belonged to God to begin with.

This week we have walked through the Lord’s Prayer: knowing the Father, hallowing his name, letting God reign, relying on his provision and living out forgiveness, and finally giving the glory to God. Building what belongs to God means fulfilling the Lord’s Prayer. Next week we will go deeper into a key truth: for God’s kingdom to come, we must first return to our place—humility.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One purpose—building what belongs to God means giving the kingdom, the power and the glory entirely to God. Self-ruled people want a share of the pie, keeping a little power and a little glory for themselves; self-emptied people gladly give it all to the Lord. Giving glory to God and thanks in everything is the destination of the path of service.
q: Who is God? — “All that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours”: how does this shape the way you view everything you own?
Who am I? — What portion of power or glory are you secretly trying to keep for yourself?
How shall I respond? — When you finish a task today, how will you give the glory to God?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted, Satan offered him the glory of all the kingdoms of the world if only he would bow down and worship. Jesus refused that shortcut and chose the cross. After his resurrection he said, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” He walked the road of humility and received the true kingdom and glory.
lessons.pray: Lord, yours is the kingdom, the power and the glory forever. Everything I have comes from you, and everything I accomplish is your grace. Deliver me from the evil one, and take away the pride in my heart that wants a share of your glory. May I live my whole life only for your kingdom and your glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pray through the whole Lord’s Prayer once in your own words
Each time you finish a task today, pray silently: “Glory to you”
At the weekend, pray the Lord’s Prayer together with a spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever.” — Lord, right now all glory goes to you.

mem.t: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

lessons.title: Pride: Leaving Our Place
lessons.theme: The root of pride is refusing to treat God as God

v: Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened.
Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.

lessons.still: Quietly ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: “Lord, where have I put myself in your place?” Don’t rush to answer; let one or two pictures slowly come to mind. There is no need to be afraid—his light is where healing begins.
teach: As long as a train stays on its tracks, it can travel smoothly and fast; once it “fights for freedom” and leaves the rails, it overturns. Human beings also have a place God has set for us: created people under the Creator God. Pride is leaving that track, thinking that derailing is freedom—but the result is destruction.

Paul points to the root of humanity’s problem: “knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks.” Pride is not necessarily strutting arrogance; more fundamentally, it is not treating God as God—not glorifying him, not thanking him, and making ourselves the centre. Proverbs warns that “pride goes before destruction”: before every fall there is a heart lifted up.

Pride wears many faces: always thinking we are right, needing to save face, being unteachable, envy, ingratitude—even excessive self-loathing, which is still centred on self. The simplest question for spotting pride is: “Who is sitting on the throne right now? Who is getting the glory?” Seeing it is the first step towards humility.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our place and grasping power. At the core of self-rule is the desire to take God’s place. Ingratitude is a symptom of pride, and giving thanks in everything is where returning to our place begins; only when we treat God as God can we truly be human.
q: Who is God? — God deserves to be “glorified as God”; what does this mean for you?
Who am I? — Which face does pride most often wear in you?
How shall I respond? — What act of thanksgiving will you use today to put God back on the throne?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am gentle and humble in heart.” He is Lord of all, yet on earth he never left his place as the obedient Son of Man; everything he said and did followed the Father’s command. In him we see what humanity was created to be: wholly dependent on God and wholly glorifying God.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often know you, yet do not glorify you as God or give you thanks. Shine your light on the hidden pride within me, and forgive my heart that wants to sit on the throne. Today I return to my place as your creature, acknowledging that you are God, and I am the one you made and love. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down one face of pride in your life, and confess it to the Lord
Today, express five specific thanks—to God and to people
When someone corrects you, first say, “Thank you for pointing that out,” and only then explain
lessons.noon: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” — Lord, right now I return to my place.

lessons.title: The Tax Collector’s Prayer
lessons.theme: Humility is laying down power and returning to our place as sinners who receive grace

v: But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,

lessons.still: Like the tax collector, bow your head, place your hand gently on your chest, and say just one sentence: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Repeat it several times, and let it become the posture of your heart, not just words on your lips.
teach: If a judge comes home and keeps passing judgement on his wife and children, there will be little warmth in that home. If a manager still expects everyone to follow orders after work, friends gradually drift away. Power itself is not the problem; the problem is using it where it doesn’t belong, or clinging to it. Humility starts with laying down the power that isn’t ours to hold.

The Pharisee “stood” and reported his achievements to God—and passed judgement on the tax collector while he was at it. He had seized the power to judge others. The tax collector “stood far away” and would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, asking only for God’s mercy. Jesus said it was this man who went home justified. Humility is not putting ourselves down; it is honestly standing in our place as sinners who receive grace.

Peter says, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God.” Humility is an active choice: laying down the power of “I’m better than you,” the power of “I must win,” the power of “I have the final say,” and returning to God’s hand. In due time, God will lift up the humble—lifting up is God’s part; humbling ourselves is ours.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our place—let people be people and let God be God. The Pharisee made himself the judge: that is pride. The tax collector admitted he needed grace: that is the self-emptied life. The humble are the best receivers of grace, because only empty hands can catch a gift.
q: Who is God? — What kind of prayer most pleases a God who “gives grace to the humble”?
Who am I? — Are you more prone to compare yourself like the Pharisee, or to beat your breast like the tax collector?
How shall I respond? — What kind of power that you cling to will you lay down today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus often ate with tax collectors and sinners, yet he sharply exposed the self-righteous. He himself was without any sin, yet he willingly stood with sinners to be baptised in the Jordan, and in the end he was counted among criminals. His humility made the lowliest dare to come near, and left the proud with nowhere to hide.
lessons.pray: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. I confess that I am often like the Pharisee, comparing, judging and boasting about myself. Today I lay down the power to judge others and the power of needing to win, and I humble myself under your mighty hand. When and how I am lifted up, I leave to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: When you pray today, say only the tax collector’s sentence, and quietly receive grace
Notice every thought of comparing yourself with others, and hand each one to the Lord
In a discussion, deliberately let others finish speaking and decide first
lessons.noon: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” — Lord, right now I lay myself down and look only to your grace.

lessons.title: He Must Increase, I Must Decrease
lessons.theme: Letting people be people and God be God is the most secure place to stand

v: He must increase, but I must decrease.
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

lessons.still: Quietly consider: which of today’s matters are your responsibility, and which are God’s? In your heart, sort them into two piles. Tell the Lord, “My part I will do faithfully; your part I hand over to you.”
teach: At a wedding, the best man’s role is clear: to help, to stand by, and to rejoice for the groom. If the best man tries to steal the groom’s spotlight, the wedding becomes a farce. John the Baptist compared himself to the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices greatly when he hears the bridegroom’s voice. He knew who he was, and he knew who the main character was.

When his disciples were worried that everyone was going over to Jesus, John said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” This is not a loser consoling himself; it is the joy of someone who knows his place. Micah describes our human place very simply: act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God—not walking ahead of God, nor lagging behind, but walking “with” him.

Letting people be people means accepting our limits: we are not all-knowing, not all-powerful, and certainly not the saviour of the world. Letting God be God means handing outcomes, evaluations and other people’s change over to him. Much of our anxiety and exhaustion comes from trying to carry God’s load. When we return to our place, our shoulders actually grow lighter.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our place—let people be people and let God be God. The self-emptied life does not mean being nothing; it means living out the infinite from our proper place. John gladly decreased, yet Jesus said that among those born of women none was greater than John the Baptist.
q: Who is God? — Why does God delight to walk with those who “walk humbly”?
Who am I? — In what matter are you trying to carry a load that only God can carry?
How shall I respond? — What will you let “decrease” today so that Jesus may “increase”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Even the Son of God, while on earth, gladly kept to his place as the one sent. He let the Father be the Father, and the Father exalted him and gave him the name above every name.
lessons.pray: Lord, you must increase, and I must decrease. Save me from the heart that wants to be the main character, and save me from the burden of trying to carry everything. I am willing to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with you. My part I will do faithfully; all the rest I place in your hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Make two columns, “My responsibility” and “God’s responsibility,” and entrust the second to him
Today, sincerely praise a co-worker’s or family member’s achievement
In one matter, give the credit to someone else or to God
lessons.noon: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” — Lord, right now I gladly step back behind you.

lessons.title: The Lord Who Picked Up the Towel
lessons.theme: True authority is for stooping down to serve

v: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus kneeling in front of you, holding your dusty feet in his hands. Do you want to pull them back? Quietly receive his service. Then consider: whose feet do I need to wash today?
teach: In ancient times most roads were dirt tracks and people wore sandals; washing guests’ feet at the door was the job of the lowest servant in the house. That night the disciples were still arguing about who was the greatest, and no one was willing to pick up the towel. In the end, the one who picked up the towel was their Lord.

John deliberately spells out the setting of the foot-washing: Jesus knew “that the Father had given all things into his hands.” Jesus did not serve because he lacked authority; it was precisely because he was sure of his authority and identity that he could lay that authority down to serve. Proud people fear losing their status, so they will not stoop; only those secure in the Father’s love dare to kneel.

The Lord said, “I have given you an example.” Foot-washing is not merely a ritual but a way of life: doing what nobody wants to do, serving people who cannot repay you, and being gentle with others’ weaknesses. Humility is not sitting there thinking about how lowly we are; it is getting up and picking up the towel.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example. True authority is not for being served but for serving—this is what it means to serve under the Lord’s authority. Humility inspires humility: when someone picks up the towel first, the atmosphere of arguing over who is greatest is turned upside down.
q: Who is God? — The Lord of all kneels to wash feet; how does this change the way you understand God’s greatness?
Who am I? — When do you find yourself thinking, “That’s not my job”?
How shall I respond? — Whose “feet” will you wash today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus washed the feet of all his disciples—including Judas, who would betray him, and Peter, who would deny him three times. His service did not depend on whether people deserved it; it flowed from a heart that “loved them to the end.” This same Lord still washes us clean today.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are Lord of lords, yet you picked up a towel and washed your disciples’ feet. I often argue about who is greatest and keep score of who should serve whom. Let me feel secure in your love, so that I dare to stoop down and serve. Today, lead me to wash a pair of feet that need washing. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Take the initiative to do a small task at home or in your fellowship that nobody wants to do
Serve someone who cannot repay you
Show a specific kindness to someone who has made you uncomfortable
lessons.noon: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” — Lord, right now I am willing to stoop down.

lessons.title: Revival Begins with Humbling Ourselves
lessons.theme: Humility is the key that opens the door to revival

v: if my people who are called by my name will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
