For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.

lessons.still: Quietly kneel or bow your head and say to the Lord, “Lord, let revival begin with me.” Ask the Holy Spirit to point out one place where you need to humble yourself and repent. Today, before praying for anyone else, pray for your own heart.
teach: However small a key is, if its teeth are cut right, it can open a heavy door; with the wrong key, no amount of force will open it. We often try to bring revival through more activities and better strategies, but the key God gives is simple: humbling ourselves.

After Solomon dedicated the temple, God promised: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways,” he would hear, forgive and heal. Notice that the first verb is “humble themselves.” Isaiah also says that the high and holy God dwells with those who are contrite and humble in spirit, to revive them. God dwells in the highest place—and in the lowest.

This week we have seen that pride is leaving our place; humility is laying down power; we let people be people and God be God; and Jesus picked up the towel. Revival does not start with changing others; it starts with my own humility. Next week we will see that humility is not only a virtue but a weapon in spiritual warfare, overcoming pride and Satan.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is the key to revival. Revival in families, churches and workplaces always begins with one person laying down power and returning to their place. Humility inspires humility and brings a win for everyone; when one person kneels, the hearts of many are often opened.
q: Who is God? — How do you understand that God “dwells in the high and holy place” and also “with him who is of a humble spirit”?
Who am I? — Are you expecting revival to start with others rather than with yourself?
How shall I respond? — In which relationship will you be the first to open the door with humility today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus existed in the form of God, yet he went all the way down: born in a manger, washing his disciples’ feet, dying on a cross. And for that very reason God exalted him to the highest place. Resurrection life springs up from the lowest place; this is the most fundamental road to revival.
lessons.pray: High and holy God, thank you that you are willing to dwell with those who are contrite and humble in spirit. I long for revival, and I know it must begin with me. I humble myself before you and turn away from my pride and self-righteousness. Hear me, forgive me and heal me; revive my spirit. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Memorise this week’s verse: James 4:6
Take the initiative to apologise to a family member or co-worker about one matter
Pray for revival in your family or church, beginning by confessing your own sin
lessons.noon: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit.” — Lord, right now I humble myself before you.

mem.t: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

lessons.title: The Fall of the Shining One
lessons.theme: Satan’s very nature is the proud desire to be equal with God

v: How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low!
You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north!
I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!”

lessons.still: Quietly acknowledge: “Lord, spiritual warfare is real, but you have already won.” Hand your fears to the Lord, and ask him for a sober mind to see through the enemy’s schemes, without ever making the enemy bigger than the Lord.
teach: To treat an illness, a doctor must first identify what is causing it; get the cause wrong, and even the best medicine won’t help. Many of the symptoms in our spiritual lives—quarrels, bitterness, anxiety, self-indulgence—often have the same underlying cause: pride. To overcome, we must first recognise the original form of this disease.

Isaiah describes the arrogance of the king of Babylon, and in it we glimpse the proud spirit behind him: five times he says “I will”—I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of assembly, I will ascend above the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High. This is the prototype of self-rule: a creature trying to seize the Creator’s place. And it ends with “How you have fallen from heaven!”

When that ancient serpent said to humanity in Eden, “You will be like God,” he was passing his own disease on to us. So the heart of spiritual warfare is not mysterious phenomena but the battle over “who reigns.” Every time I insist on “I will,” I am in tune with the enemy; every time I say “What you desire,” I am standing on God’s side.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our place and grasping power—and Satan was the first to do it. Self-rule is Satan’s nature; the self-emptied life is Christ’s nature. Once we see this clearly, we understand why humility overcomes pride, and the self-emptied life overcomes Satan.
q: Who is God? — God brings the proud one “fallen from heaven”; what does this reveal about his justice and sovereignty?
Who am I? — Which “I will”s in your life actually sound like the enemy’s voice?
How shall I respond? — Which “I will” will you change into “What you desire” today?
lessons.jesus: The enemy said, “I will ascend into heaven,” but Jesus came down from heaven. The enemy wanted to be equal with God, but Jesus “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.” The two roads are complete opposites: one climbs upward and falls; the other goes downward and is exalted to the highest place. Following Jesus means taking the downward road.
lessons.pray: Lord, I see the root of pride, and I see the “I will” that so often fills my heart. Forgive me for the times I have been in tune with the enemy. I don’t want to climb up high to be equal with you; I want to follow Jesus on the downward road. Keep me, so that I overcome in the place you have set for me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three “I will”s you have said this week, and hand each one to the Lord
When a quarrel arises today, first ask: “Whose voice is this?”
Read Isaiah 14:12–15 and pray over your own heart
lessons.noon: “I will make myself like the Most High!” — Lord, right now I will not exalt myself; I want only you to be God.

lessons.title: The Cycle of Biting and Devouring
lessons.theme: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose

v: Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice.
But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another.

lessons.still: Think back to your most recent conflict. Don’t analyse who was right or wrong; simply look, in the Lord’s presence, at what your own heart was like at the time. Quietly ask, “Lord, back then, did I want to win, or did I want to love?”
teach: Two goats meet in the middle of a narrow log bridge. Neither will give way; they butt horns back and forth until both tumble into the river. Proud conflicts go just like that: you get louder, I get louder still; you go cold, I go colder. Each person feels they are only “responding,” and together they fall into the river.

Proverbs says, “Pride only breeds quarrels.” The root of an argument is often not the issue itself but the heart that says, “I can’t lose.” Paul warned the Galatian church: “If you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another.” James goes straight to the root: fights and quarrels come from the desires that battle within us. Pride provokes pride, and in the end there is no winner.

The key to breaking the cycle is to see clearly our own role in it. Rather than waiting for the other person to change first, ask: “Are my words putting out the fire, or adding fuel?” Deal with your own pride first—not because you must be the one in the wrong, but because you are the only party you can control.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and brings a win for everyone. The focus is not on others’ faults but on my own heart. People matter more than things; don’t hurt a person just to win an argument.
q: Who is God? — When God sees his children “biting and devouring” one another, what is his heart like?
Who am I? — In conflict, what is your most common way of “adding fuel”?
How shall I respond? — In which tense relationship will you be the first to stop trying to win?
lessons.jesus: All along the road the disciples argued about who was the greatest. Jesus did not join the argument; instead he called a little child to stand among them and taught them what true greatness is. When he was insulted, he did not insult in return; when he suffered, he made no threats. By refusing to strike back, he broke the cycle of pride.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that in conflict I often want to win and answer pride with pride, hurting others and myself. Forgive my biting and devouring words. Give me the courage to be the first to stop, the first to let go, the first to cool things down. In every relationship, make me someone who puts out fires, not someone who adds fuel. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before speaking today, ask: “Will this put out the fire or add fuel?”
With someone you have recently clashed with, drop one point you “must win”
When you feel offended, silently count to ten and pray to the Lord
lessons.noon: “Pride only breeds quarrels.” — Lord, right now I lay down my need to win.

lessons.title: Jacob and Esau
lessons.theme: Humility inspires humility, and relationships become a win for both

v: He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.still: Think of someone with whom there is distance between you. Quietly, before the Lord, speak one sentence of blessing over them. Then ask the Lord to show you a way to take one small, humble step towards them.
teach: A hammer cannot break through a frozen lake, but the sun can slowly melt it. The walls of ice between people are the same: meeting force with force only sends shards flying, but gentleness and humility can turn hard ice into flowing water.

Jacob had once cheated his brother out of his blessing. Twenty years later, on his way home, he heard that Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men, and he trembled with fear. At the ford of the Jabbok he wrestled with God; he came away limping, and his life was changed. When he met his brother, he no longer played tricks; instead he bowed to the ground seven times. And Esau ran to embrace him, and they both wept. Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath.”

Humility does not guarantee that the other person will change immediately, but it changes the atmosphere and gives the other person a way to step down gracefully. Pride leaves both sides with no way to back down; humility gives both sides a way forward. Spiritual victory is not “I win, you lose,” but God receiving glory and people receiving blessing.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility inspires humility and brings a win for everyone. The 920 life: every person in my life is my “2”; I practise the “0” of the self-emptied life; and the result is the “9”—the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.
q: Who is God? — God first changed Jacob at the Jabbok and then restored the brothers’ relationship; what does this show you about how God works?
Who am I? — In which relationship are you still “playing tricks” instead of being humble?
How shall I respond? — Towards which of “my 2” will you take one small, humble step?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not speak coldly to Peter after his fall. Instead he prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast on the shore and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” His gentleness raised up a man who had failed and restored a broken relationship.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for changing Jacob first, and for changing me again and again. Take away my heart that plays tricks and meets force with force in relationships, and give me a gentle answer that turns away wrath. Help me, in one difficult relationship, to be the first to bow and the first to lower my head, so that you receive glory and both of us are blessed. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Reach out to someone you have drifted apart from, and send a word of greeting
When someone talks back to you today, answer once in a gentle tone
Write down three things to be thankful for in the “2” you find hardest to get along with
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath.” — Lord, right now let my words carry your gentleness.

lessons.title: Submit and Resist
lessons.theme: Only when we first submit to God can we resist the devil

v: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.
Withstand him steadfast in your faith, knowing that your brothers who are in the world are undergoing the same sufferings.

lessons.still: Say quietly, “Lord, I submit to you.” Hand over to him today’s plans, emotions and weaknesses one by one. Then, with a clear mind, declare: “In Christ I do not fear the enemy, because you have already won.”
teach: If a soldier ignores his commander’s orders and charges onto the battlefield on his own, however brave he is, he will only die in vain. Spiritual warfare also has an order: “Be subject to God” comes first, and “resist the devil” comes second. Resistance without submission is just human bravado; with submission, resistance carries authority.

James sets out the order clearly: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God. Peter says the devil is like a roaring lion and calls us to be sober and watchful and to resist him, steadfast in faith. Notice that both apostles speak first about humility and then about warfare—“God resists the proud,” “Humble yourselves.” Humility is the very foundation for resisting the devil.

The enemy’s favourite doors are pride, bitterness, unforgiveness and fear. Submitting to God means shutting those doors. Resisting is not a matter of a loud voice or special rituals; it is a matter of truth: like Jesus, answering lies with “It is written,” and drawing near to God, staying in his presence.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus reign—serve by his authority, and fight by his authority. Self-ruled people want to fight their battles themselves; self-emptied people obey the Commander. Humility overcomes pride; the self-emptied life overcomes Satan—victory lies not in my strength but in my submission.
q: Who is God? — “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you”: how does this promise help you know God?
Who am I? — Which door in your life may be standing open to the enemy?
How shall I respond? — Which verse will you use today to resist a lie that often troubles you?
lessons.jesus: Jesus fasted forty days and nights in the wilderness and was tempted three times. Each time he answered, “It is written,” and finally said, “Get behind me, Satan!” Because he fully submitted to the Father, he had authority to resist the enemy. This victorious Lord is with us today.
lessons.pray: Lord, I submit to you and hand over to you my thoughts, my emotions and my plans. Shut the doors in my life that stand open to the enemy—pride, bitterness and fear. By your word I resist the devil’s lies. I want to draw near to you, because you have promised to draw near to me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Memorise this week’s verse: James 4:7
Identify a lie that often troubles you, and write down a verse that answers it
When you are tempted today, first say: “Lord, I submit to you”
lessons.noon: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.” — Lord, right now I submit to you and draw near to you.

lessons.title: The Victory of the Self-Emptied Life
lessons.theme: The Lamb’s blood and the self-emptied life overcome the enemy

v: They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.
You are of God, little children, and have overcome them, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world.

lessons.still: Quietly look up to the Lamb on the cross and say, “Lord, your blood has already won.” Hand your weakness over to him; exchange your fear for trust and your burdens for praise.
teach: In chess, a player sometimes sacrifices a rook and, by doing so, checkmates the opponent’s king. The cross was the most unexpected move in history: the enemy thought he had won by having Jesus crucified, not knowing that the Lamb’s death was his own endgame. God’s victories often come in what looks like defeat.

Revelation says the believers overcame the accuser for three reasons: the Lamb’s blood, the word of their testimony, and not loving their lives even to death. The third is the self-emptied life: no longer centred on self, not clinging even to life itself. All the enemy’s weapons—accusation, intimidation, temptation—are aimed at the “self”; when a person lives the self-emptied life, he finds nothing to grip.

John says, “Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world.” This week we have seen Satan’s pride, the cycle of pride, the win-win of humility, submitting and resisting, and finally the victory of the self-emptied life. After battle we need rest; next week we will learn to enter God’s rest within the rhythm he has established.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life overcomes Satan; humility overcomes pride. Self-emptying does not mean being nothing; it means entering the infinite and living out the infinite—letting the Greater One live in me. A defeated life becomes an overcoming life, and the key is who reigns.
q: Who is God? — “Greater is he who is in you”: how does this change the way you see your own battles?
Who am I? — Which part of your “self” does the enemy most often target: your pride, your rights, or your comfort?
How shall I respond? — To whom will you testify about something God has done today?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus seemed to be defeated, but in fact he was winning. Paul says that through the cross he triumphed over all rulers and authorities and took them captive. By giving himself up, he overcame the proud enemy. His victory is already complete, and we fight from within his victory.
lessons.pray: Victorious Lamb, thank you for overcoming the enemy by your own blood. Greater is he who is in me than he who is in the world. Free me from the heart that clings to self, so that I do not hold on to my pride, my rights or my comfort, but let you alone live in me. May I stand in your victory every day. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Share with a friend one victory God has won in your life
Today, lay down your rights in one matter and hand it to the Lord
At the weekend, pray together with a spiritual companion for each other’s battles
lessons.noon: “Because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world.” — Lord, right now I stand in your victory.

mem.t: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.

lessons.title: The Rest of the Seventh Day
lessons.theme: Rest is a gift God built into creation

v: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.

lessons.still: Put down whatever is in your hands. Sit back in your chair and let your shoulders drop. Tell the Lord, “Lord, you rested from your work on the seventh day; today I too will rest a while before you.” Quietly enjoy the freedom of this moment, when there is nothing you have to do.
teach: A musical score has rests in it. They are not mistakes but part of the music; a piece with no rests would be nothing but noise. In the rhythm of creation, God also wrote in a rest: the seventh day.

God rested from his work not because he was tired, but because the work was finished and he wanted to enjoy the goodness of what he had made. He “blessed the seventh day, and made it holy”—the first thing in the Bible that God set apart as holy was not a place but a span of time. The Ten Commandments also say, “Remember the Sabbath day,” reminding us that we are not machines but living beings made in God’s image, who need rhythm.

People today see rest as a waste and busyness as a mark of worth. Our mindset needs to change: rest is not a reward for work but God’s command and God’s gift. It declares, “I am not God; the world keeps turning without me.” Being willing to stop is acknowledging that God is in control.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Refusing to rest is often the other face of self-rule—thinking everything depends on me. Rest is returning to our human place: let people be people and let God be God. As our perspective shifts from the temporary to the eternal, even our time becomes part of building what belongs to God.
q: Who is God? — God “blessed the seventh day”; what does this show you about his care for people?
Who am I? — Do you often feel that stopping is a waste—or even feel guilty about it?
How shall I respond? — At what time this week will you deliberately set your work aside?
lessons.jesus: Jesus regularly went to the synagogue on the Sabbath, and on the Sabbath he also healed the sick and set people free. He said, “My Father is still working, so I am working too.” He turned the Sabbath from a rule that binds people into a day when God restores people and makes them whole.
lessons.pray: Creator God, thank you for placing the gift of rest within time. I confess that I often treat busyness as my worth and refuse to stop. Teach me to remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy, and when I stop, to acknowledge that you are God. May my life follow your rhythm rather than being driven by anxiety. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Set aside thirty minutes today with no work and no scrolling
Write down one piece of work you can let go of and hand over to God
Choose a full block of rest this week and write it in your calendar
lessons.noon: “God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy.” — Lord, right now I rest a while in you.

lessons.title: Taking the Lord’s Yoke
lessons.theme: Exchange your yoke for Jesus’ yoke, and your soul will find rest

v: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

lessons.still: Imagine you are carrying a heavy pack, filled with responsibilities, expectations and worries. In front of Jesus, take them out one by one and set them down. Then hear him say, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me.” Receive the light burden he hands you.
teach: In ancient times a yoke was a wooden frame fitted across an ox’s shoulders. A good carpenter would shape each yoke to fit its ox, so that it sat well and didn’t chafe. Jesus worked as a carpenter in Nazareth, and when he says, “My yoke is easy,” the word also carries the sense of “well-fitting, good to use”—the burden he gives is made to measure.

Jesus’ invitation is not “You don’t have to carry anything,” but “Change your yoke.” The yoke we were carrying was our own: proving ourselves, pleasing people, controlling everything. Jesus says, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me”—he is the one who shares the yoke with us and leads the way. The secret lies in “I am gentle and humble in heart”: rest comes from learning his humility.

Much of our weariness is not because there is too much to do, but because our pride is too heavy: needing to save face, needing to be perfect, needing others to do things my way. Taking up the Lord’s yoke means laying down these self-imposed burdens and sharing the yoke with him. The work is still there, but our souls find rest.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our place—this is exactly Jesus’ yoke. The yoke of self-rule is as heavy as a millstone; the yoke of the self-emptied life is easy and light. Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself: share the yoke with the Lord, and living from the heart brings joy.
q: Who is God? — What does a Lord who says “Come to me” mean for you in your weariness?
Who am I? — What “yoke of your own” are you carrying on your shoulders that the Lord never asked you to carry?
How shall I respond? — Which aspect of Jesus’ “gentle and humble” way will you learn today?
lessons.jesus: Just before giving this invitation, Jesus had been rejected by many towns, yet he said, “Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight.” His rest came from wholly accepting the Father’s will. He carried the heaviest cross of all, so that we could carry his light yoke.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I labour and am heavily burdened, often carrying yokes you never asked me to carry. Today I come to you and lay down the burden of proving myself and controlling everything. I am willing to take your yoke and learn your gentle and humble ways. Let my soul find rest even in the midst of my work. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down one “yoke of your own,” and beside it write: “Given to the Lord”
As you do a task today, pray silently: “Lord, let’s do this together”
Memorise this week’s verse: Matthew 11:28
lessons.noon: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened.” — Lord, right now I come to you.

lessons.title: The Faith to Stop
lessons.theme: Stopping means trusting that God is more reliable than I am

v: Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.
There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God.
For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and call to mind, one by one, the things you haven’t finished today. For each one, say, “Lord, you watch over this.” Then breathe in deeply and breathe out slowly, and let your body truly relax.
teach: A baby sleeps soundly in its mother’s arms—not because it has solved all its problems, but because it trusts the one holding it. Adults often sleep poorly, because we think that the moment we close our eyes, the world will spin out of control.

Psalm 127 says that unless the Lord builds and watches over, it is “vain” to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil; “for he gives sleep to his loved ones.” Sleep becomes an act of faith. Hebrews says that those who enter his rest have “rested from their works”—not that they no longer work, but that they no longer rely on their work to be saved or to have worth.

Stopping takes faith: trusting that God is still at work while I rest. The greatest temptation in our work is to think that success or failure rests entirely on us. Being willing to stop when it is time to stop is saying to God, “You are the builder; I am your co-worker.” Rest like this keeps us from being swallowed by busyness or crushed by failure.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Everything is what God has done and accomplished in Jesus; all of it is grace. Resting from our own works is the mark of a life of grace; refusing to stop because everything depends on me is the mark of self-rule. When we let Jesus reign, even our sleep becomes trust and worship.
q: Who is God? — “He gives sleep to his loved ones”: what does this show you about God’s love?
Who am I? — Do you feel that success or failure rests entirely on you?
How shall I respond? — Tonight, how will you express your trust by “sleeping in peace”?
lessons.jesus: A great storm arose on the Sea of Galilee and the boat was about to sink, yet Jesus was asleep in the stern. His sleep was not irresponsibility but complete trust in the Father. When his panicked disciples cried out, he got up, calmed the storm, and asked them why they were afraid. He invites us, too, to rest in the storm.
lessons.pray: Lord, unless you build the house, all my labour is in vain. I often think that if I stop, things will fall apart, so I sleep poorly at night. Today I hand my unfinished tasks to you to watch over, and I rest from my own works. Let me sleep in peace like a baby in its mother’s arms. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before bed, write down three things for tomorrow, then pray and entrust them to God
Set a time to stop work today, and when it comes, really stop
About one thing you cannot control, say: “Lord, you watch over this”
lessons.noon: “For he gives sleep to his loved ones.” — Lord, right now I place my burdens in your hands.

lessons.title: The Lord’s Day: Worship and Renewal
lessons.theme: The Lord’s Day is a day to be renewed together with God and his people

v: He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”
Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works,
not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.

lessons.still: Think back to last Sunday: did you rush in late with your mind elsewhere, or did you come with a heart prepared to worship? Quietly tell the Lord, “Lord, this Lord’s Day I want to come before you with a prepared heart.”
teach: Phones need charging every day, and cars need regular servicing; otherwise even the best machine will break down halfway. The Lord’s Day is like regular servicing for the soul: meeting with God, gathering with brothers and sisters, resting body and mind, and then setting out again.

Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” Rest is not a burden but a gift; and he is “lord even of the Sabbath”—he himself is the centre of our rest. The early church gathered to break bread on the first day of the week, the day the Lord rose. Hebrews reminds us not to forsake meeting together, but to consider how to spur one another on to love and good works.

The Lord’s Day has two emphases: worship and rest. Worship refocuses the whole week on God; rest is trusting God’s provision. Don’t let the Lord’s Day become another busy workday, and don’t treat it merely as a holiday for sleeping till noon. It is a day to be renewed together with God and with his people.
lessons.light: 321 Light: First with God, then with people, then with tasks. Sunday worship is the day we realign the order of our relationships; caring for one another is the 235 life of walking with spiritual companions. Letting Jesus receive all the glory begins with Sunday worship and extends into every day of the week.
q: Who is God? — Jesus is “lord even of the Sabbath”; what does this mean for your Lord’s Day?
Who am I? — Is your Lord’s Day more like recharging and servicing, or just another kind of busyness?
How shall I respond? — This Lord’s Day, how will you prepare your heart to worship and also truly rest?
lessons.jesus: On the Sabbath Jesus went into the synagogue “as was his custom” and worshipped with the people. He rose on the first day of the week and appeared to his disciples and was with them. He is not only Lord of the Sabbath; he is the Lord who is with us when we gather.
lessons.pray: Lord of the Sabbath, thank you for giving me the Lord’s Day to service and renew my soul. Help me not to forsake meeting together, to come with a heart prepared to worship you, and to care for my brothers and sisters. May my Lord’s Day not be stolen by busyness, but be a day of rest and strength in you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Go to bed early the night before the Lord’s Day, and prepare your heart to worship
This Lord’s Day, reach out to someone at church who is often overlooked
Set aside time on the Lord’s Day to rest well with your family
lessons.noon: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” — Lord, right now I am renewed in you.

lessons.title: The Rhythm of Life
lessons.theme: Living by God’s rhythm makes for a spiritual life that lasts

v: He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

lessons.still: Take out your calendar or phone and quietly look over this week’s schedule. Ask the Lord, “Which of these do you want me to do? Where do I need to stop?” Let the Holy Spirit point out one place that needs adjusting.
teach: The heart contracts and relaxes, never stopping for a lifetime, because it has a rhythm: every contraction is followed by relaxation. A heart that only contracted and never relaxed would fail. Spiritual life needs rhythm too: work and rest, service and retreat, community and solitude, taking their turns.

When the disciples came back from their preaching mission, they were so busy they didn’t even have time to eat. So Jesus said, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” The Lord not only sends people out to work; he personally leads them to rest. Moses prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” Rhythm means using wisely the days God gives us.

Over these seven weeks we have built the basic practices: coming home, stillness, Scripture, prayer, humility, victory and rest. Now we arrange them into a workable rhythm: daily stillness, Bible reading and prayer; the weekly Lord’s Day and Sabbath rest; and a quarterly retreat and review. Next week we will see the foundation beneath it all: the assurance of salvation.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset and your life will change; change your life and the way you live will change. Rhythm means writing truth into the schedule of our lives. When we practise, review, correct and repeat regularly, our lives grow steadily, building what belongs to God step by step.
q: Who is God? — The Lord says, “Come… and rest awhile”; what does this show you about his considerate care?
Who am I? — Is your current rhythm of life more like a heart that contracts and relaxes, or one that only contracts and never relaxes?
How shall I respond? — What daily and weekly rhythm will you write down for yourself?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ life had a clear rhythm: praying alone in the early morning, serving among the crowds by day, going to the synagogue on the Sabbath, and often taking his disciples away to quiet places. He was never driven by needs, but acted according to the Father’s timing. He is the model for the rhythm of our lives.
lessons.pray: Lord, teach me to count my days, that I may gain a heart of wisdom. My life often only contracts and never relaxes; I am so busy I don’t even have time to be with you. Help me to build a rhythm that belongs to you: drawing near to you every day, resting and worshipping every week, and often going away with you to rest awhile. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down your daily rhythm: what time you will be still, read Scripture and pray
Mark this week’s rest time and the Lord’s Day on your calendar
Share your rhythm of life with a spiritual companion and ask them to check in weekly
lessons.noon: “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” — Lord, right now I go with you to rest awhile.

mem.t: These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may continue to believe in the name of the Son of God.

lessons.title: Assurance Built on a Promise
lessons.theme: The assurance of salvation rests on God’s word, not on our feelings

v: The testimony is this: that God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life.
These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may continue to believe in the name of the Son of God.
“Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.

lessons.still: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, like someone receiving a gift that has already arrived. Slowly say three times: “He who has the Son has the life.” Each time you say it, hand the Lord one “what if I’m not good enough?” thought.
teach: When you fly, a lurch in your stomach doesn’t convince you that you are no longer on the plane. Whether you are on board depends on your boarding pass and the aircraft, not on how you feel. The spiritual life works the same way: feelings are like the weather, sunny one day and rainy the next, but assurance must be built on a foundation that does not change.

John states his purpose plainly: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Not “hope,” not “guess,” but “know.” On what basis? “He who has the Son has the life.” Eternal life is not a thing; it is found in a Person. Jesus himself said that whoever believes “has passed out of death into life”—he speaks of it as already done.

The order of assurance is: fact → faith → feeling. God’s word is the locomotive, faith is the coal car, and feeling is only the last carriage. Put feeling at the front and the whole train goes nowhere. Change your mindset and you change your life: move from “Do I feel saved?” to “What has God said?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard. Assurance does not rest on my feelings or performance but on God’s word. Making feelings the standard puts “me” at the center; making God’s word the standard lets God be God. The self-ruled person is often dragged about by emotions; the self-emptied person rests in God’s faithfulness.
q: Who is God? — What kind of God writes his promises down because he wants you to “know”?
Who am I? — Does your assurance of salvation usually rest on feelings, on performance, or on God’s word?
How shall I respond? — Today, when doubt rises up, which verse will you answer it with?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never left people living in guesswork. To the repentant thief on the cross he said, “Today you will be with me in Paradise.” That man had no time to do good works or make amends—only a faith that turned toward Jesus—yet he received the clearest promise of all. Assurance comes from Jesus’ words, not from our résumé.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you that you do not leave me living in guesswork and anxiety. You said that whoever has your Son has life—so I have life. When my feelings waver, bring me back to stand firm on your word. I do not rely on my own performance, but only on the finished work of Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write 1 John 5:13 on a card and put it where you will see it often
Write down one feeling that often makes you doubt your salvation, and next to it write a promise from Scripture
Tell a brother or sister in Christ: “I know I have eternal life, because…”
lessons.noon: “He who has the Son has the life.” — Lord, right now I look not at my feelings but at your word.

lessons.title: No One Can Snatch Them
lessons.theme: The Good Shepherd holds his sheep and never lets go

v: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand.

lessons.still: Make a loose fist with one hand, then wrap your other hand around it. Picture the Father’s hand enfolding Jesus’ hand, with you held in the middle. Be still for a minute and say to the Lord, “I am in your hands. I am safe.”
teach: When a small child crosses the street, his safety does not depend on how tightly he holds his father’s hand but on how tightly his father holds his. Small hands get tired and let go; the big hand does not. Much of believers’ anxiety comes from constantly checking whether their own grip is tight enough, while forgetting to look at the great hand that is holding them.

Jesus describes his sheep with three marks: they “hear my voice,” “I know them,” and they “follow me.” Then come three guarantees: “I give eternal life to them,” “they will never perish,” and “no one will snatch them out of my hand.” More wonderful still, the sheep are in the Son’s hand and also in the Father’s hand—two hands, double protection. “No one” includes Satan, circumstances, and even your own weakness.

The sheep’s safety lies not in the sheep’s strength but in the shepherd’s faithfulness. This is no license for careless living, because true sheep hear the shepherd’s voice and follow him. Assurance and following are two sides of one coin: the more we listen to his voice, the more we know we belong to him; the more we know we belong to him, the more gladly we follow.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The focus is on Jesus, not on myself. The self-ruled person builds security on how tightly he holds on; the self-emptied person entrusts his security to the Good Shepherd. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him take responsibility for keeping me. My place is to listen and follow; his place is to hold and protect.
q: Who is God? — The Father’s hand over the Son’s hand: how does this picture help you understand God’s keeping power?
Who am I? — Do you often find yourself checking whether you are “holding on tightly enough”?
How shall I respond? — In what matter today will you quietly listen for the Good Shepherd’s voice?
lessons.jesus: Before his suffering, Jesus prayed to the Father that he had kept all those the Father had given him (John 17:12). When the soldiers came to the garden to arrest him, he stepped forward and told them to let his disciples go (John 18:8). The Good Shepherd always stands between his sheep and danger—and in the end he laid down his life for them.
lessons.pray: Jesus, Good Shepherd, thank you that you know me and hold me in your hand. My hands grow weak, but yours never let go. Make my ears more familiar with your voice and my steps more willing to follow you. Today I rest in your hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pray a “hands-enfolded” prayer, asking the Lord to keep everything in your day
Before making a decision today, pause and ask, “Lord, what do you say?”
Send John 10:28 to a friend who is feeling discouraged
lessons.noon: “And no one will snatch them out of my hand.” — Lord, right now I am secure in your hands.

lessons.title: The Spirit Bears Witness
lessons.theme: God’s Spirit within me cries, “Abba, Father”

v: For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”
The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God;
and if children, then heirs— heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him.

lessons.still: Quietly and slowly say one word: “Abba.” Add nothing else, just as a child in the dark night calls out, “Daddy.” Notice the settled peace that rises in your heart—that is the Holy Spirit bearing witness within you.
teach: Some adopted children, even after taking a new surname and moving into a new home, still hide bread under their pillow at night, afraid there will be nothing to eat tomorrow. Legally they are sons and daughters, but inwardly they still live like orphans. Many Christians are the same: their identity has changed, but their mindset is still afraid.

Paul contrasts two spirits: “the spirit of bondage again to fear” and “the Spirit of adoption.” The slave’s heart asks, Have I done enough? Will I be thrown out? But the child’s heart can cry, “Abba! Father!”—a name of intimacy and trust. What is more, “the Spirit himself testifies with our spirit”: God’s word bears witness from the outside, and the Holy Spirit bears witness from within. When outside and inside agree, we know for certain that we are God’s children.

The Spirit’s witness is not a quest for some mystical emotional high; it is a growing sense of being a child of the family. When we fail, we want to come home instead of running away; when we pray, we dare to speak honestly; when we see our brothers and sisters, we feel we are one family. And this witness brings the hope of heirs—suffering with him today, glorified with him tomorrow.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. He lives in the heart, not in the head. Living from the head keeps calculating “Am I good enough?”—the more we calculate, the more troubled we become. Living from the heart by the Spirit, we can call “Abba, Father” in peace—the more we lean on him, the more joyful we become. Moving from a slave’s heart to a child’s heart is exactly the change of mindset we need.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to be called “Abba” by you. What does that reveal about his heart?
Who am I? — At what moments do you still live like a slave afraid of being thrown out?
How shall I respond? — How will you draw near to your heavenly Father as his child today?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, at his moment of deepest anguish, Jesus prayed, “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36). In the darkest night he still used the most intimate name. Today he gives us that same name and that same Spirit, so that we become heirs together with him.
lessons.pray: Abba, Father, thank you for giving me the heart of a child. I will no longer serve you out of a slave’s fear. Holy Spirit, bear witness ever more clearly in my heart, so that even when I am weak I dare to come home, and even in the night I can still call out to you. Being your child is my greatest blessing. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Three times today, softly call out in your heart, “Abba, Father!”
Write down one “slave mindset” thought and rewrite it as a “child mindset” sentence
Say something to a family member that makes them feel, “You belong here with us”
lessons.noon: “The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.” — Lord, right now I come near to you with the heart of a child.

lessons.title: Still a Child When I Fall
lessons.theme: Sin breaks our fellowship but does not change our relationship

v: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. If anyone sins, we have a Counselor with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous.

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on one failure from today or yesterday. Don’t cover it up, and don’t keep beating yourself up over it. Hand it over like a bundle of dirty laundry and say, “Lord, I was wrong.” Then take a deep breath and receive his cleansing.
teach: If a child breaks a vase, is he still his parents’ child? Of course. But that evening he may not dare to meet their eyes, and the mood around the dinner table changes. The relationship has not been broken, but the fellowship has been damaged. Only when he says, “I’m sorry—I broke it,” does laughter return to the home.

John writes to “my little children”—a family word. He hopes they will not sin, and he also provides a way back: “If anyone sins, we have a Counselor with the Father.” The word “confess” carries the sense of “saying the same thing”—standing on God’s side and seeing the matter as he sees it. God forgives on the basis of his being “faithful and righteous.” Jesus has already paid the price, so forgiveness is not God being casual about sin; it is God being just.

Before we sin, Satan says, “It’s no big deal.” After we sin, he says, “You’re finished.” Both are lies. The truth is that sin is serious—so serious that Jesus had to die; and grace is greater—so great that when we confess, we are cleansed. Don’t treat failure as a reason to leave; treat it as the road home.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When the proud fall, they cover up, make excuses and blame others—that is the self-ruled life protecting itself. The humble confess and return to their place, letting God be God. Humility is the key to revival: confession is not losing face but arriving back at the door of the Father’s house.
q: Who is God? — God’s forgiveness is “faithful and righteous.” How does that shape the way you see your own failures?
Who am I? — When you fall, is your first reaction to hide, to justify yourself, or to come home?
How shall I respond? — Is there something you need to say “I was wrong” about today, to God or to someone else?
lessons.jesus: Peter denied the Lord three times, then went out and wept bitterly. Yet the risen Jesus prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast for him on the shore and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21). Jesus did not revoke Peter’s calling; instead he entrusted him again: “Feed my sheep.” A disciple who has failed is still a disciple.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often fall, and I often want to hide from your gaze. Thank you that Jesus is my advocate and that your forgiveness is faithful and righteous. I bring my failures to you now; please cleanse me. I will no longer listen to the lie that says “You’re finished.” I am coming back to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before bed, take three minutes to review your day, and confess specifically to God any sins that come to mind
Say “I’m sorry” to someone you hurt with your words today
Memorize 1 John 1:9 and meditate on it once more before you sleep
lessons.noon: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins.” — Lord, right now I come back to you.

lessons.title: Assurance Brings Freedom
lessons.theme: We do not serve in order to be saved; we serve because we have been saved

v: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers,
nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

lessons.still: Think of a recent pressure in your ministry or work, and lay it before the Lord. Quietly tell yourself, “I am not doing this in order to be loved, but because I am already loved.” Let your shoulders slowly relax.
teach: Picture two students, both studying hard. One already knows he has been accepted; the other is still waiting for the results. Their frame of mind is completely different: the first studies in order to learn, the second studies in order to prove himself. Service without assurance is often like the second student—the more we do, the more tired and afraid we become.

At the end of Romans 8, Paul lists in one breath ten things that might separate us, and his conclusion is: none of them can. For this love is “in Christ Jesus our Lord,” firmly anchored in Christ. So he says, “be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work.” Assurance does not make us lazy; it makes us wholehearted, because “your labor is not in vain in the Lord.”

This week we have walked a path: assurance built on God’s word → held in the Good Shepherd’s hand → the Spirit’s witness → still a child when we fall → and today, serving freely from a place of assurance. Next week we will learn to “meditate day and night” on God’s word, so that this assurance can sink its roots ever deeper.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled service is about proving ourselves and winning approval; self-emptied service is for Jesus and for others. Because our salvation is settled, we don’t need to grab glory; we can let Jesus receive all the glory. Service that flows from assurance is the foundation for building what belongs to God.
q: Who is God? — “Nothing will be able to separate us from God’s love.” How secure is this God’s love?
Who am I? — How much of your service is about proving yourself?
How shall I respond? — This week, what act of service will you do in the freedom of being “already loved”?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was baptized, before he had performed a single miracle, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). He went out to serve from the Father’s affirmation, not in order to earn it. In him, we too set out from that same love.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that your love holds me fast and that nothing can separate me from you. Free me from the burden of “serving in order to be loved.” Let me set out from assurance and abound in your work freely and joyfully. All glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read Romans 8:38–39 aloud, adding the thing you fear most to the list
Do one act of service and seek no one’s praise afterward
Share with a spiritual companion one way you have become more certain of your salvation this week
lessons.noon: “Nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Lord, right now I serve freely in your love.

mem.t: This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.

lessons.title: Chewing the Cud
lessons.theme: Meditation means chewing God’s word over and over until it becomes life

v: How I love your law! It is my meditation all day.
But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart.

lessons.still: Choose one short verse, such as “Yahweh is my shepherd.” Don’t hurry on to the next line. Simply say it slowly three times, stressing a different word each time. Like a sweet held on the tongue, let its flavor slowly melt into your heart.
teach: Cattle have a peculiar habit: they swallow their grass first, then, while resting, bring it back up to chew it slowly—and only then is it truly digested. Many of us read the Bible the way we eat fast food: one gulp and we’re gone. Meditation is like chewing the cud—bringing back the word we have taken in and chewing it again and again until it becomes nourishment.

In Joshua, the Hebrew word for “meditate” carries the sense of murmuring under one’s breath, quietly repeating to oneself. The psalmist says God’s law is his “meditation all day.” Mary did the same: she did not fully understand what was happening, yet she “kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart.” Meditation is not emptying the mind but filling the heart with God’s word; it is not chasing unusual experiences but letting truth slowly unfold within us.

Reading Scripture puts food in the mouth; meditation chews it; obedience digests it into life. We often think our spiritual problem is that we haven’t read enough, but more often it is that we haven’t chewed long enough. Better to take one verse all the way in than to skim ten chapters.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself. Meditation is not analyzing with the brain and piling up knowledge; it is receiving with the heart through the Holy Spirit. Read with the head, and Scripture easily becomes exam material; read with the heart, and it becomes food. Among the eight steps of changing our mindset, “Information” must pass through meditation before it can become “Revelation.”
q: Who is God? — What patience does God show you in being willing to feed you with his word?
Who am I? — Is your Bible reading more like grabbing fast food or like chewing slowly?
How shall I respond? — Which verse will you “chew the cud” on today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he answered three times, “It is written” (Matthew 4). After forty days of fasting, God’s word came out of his mouth without his needing to open a book—the fruit of years of pondering it in his heart. He said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.”
lessons.pray: Lord, I often rush through your word without letting it into my heart. Teach me, like Mary, to keep your words and ponder them in my heart. Holy Spirit, open my heart so that your word becomes my food and turns into life within me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Choose just one verse today and meditate on it morning, noon and evening
Circle one word in the verse and ask, “What is this word saying to me?”
Before bed, write one sentence: the flavor this verse released in my heart today
lessons.noon: “How I love your law! It is my meditation all day.” — Lord, right now I chew on your word once more.

lessons.title: A Tree by the Streams
lessons.theme: Blessed is the one who meditates on God’s word day and night

v: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
but his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.

lessons.still: Picture yourself as a tree, your roots reaching downward in search of water. Quietly ask the Lord, “Where are my roots going down right now?” Then say, “Lord, I want to sink my roots into your word.”
teach: In dry country, the grass by the roadside turns brown after a few days of sun, but the tree beside the stream stays green all year round. The difference is not who tries harder but whose roots have reached the water. Meditating on God’s word means sending the roots of our life down into living water.

Psalm 1 uses three verbs to trace the gradual slide into sin: to “walk” in the counsel of the wicked, to “stand” on the path of sinners, to “sit” in the seat of scoffers—from listening, to lingering, to settling down. The blessed person turns the other way: his “delight” is in Yahweh’s law, and he “meditates day and night.” The result: fruit in its season and leaves that do not wither. Notice the word “planted”—the tree did not walk to the stream by itself; it was planted there.

Blessing does not begin with outward success but with inward “delight.” If meditation is only a duty, it soon dries up; when it becomes a delight, it becomes a day-and-night habit. Let us ask God to change our appetite, so that we love his word more than the endless stream of information on our phones.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The tree by the stream has roots first, then fruit; first a life of meditation, then a life that bears fruit. The human view looks at outward prosperity; God’s view looks at the hidden source within. Our perspective shifts from earthly things to heavenly things.
q: Who is God? — God “planted” you by the streams. What does that say about who is the source of your growth?
Who am I? — Lately, what kinds of voices have you been walking with, standing among, and sitting under?
How shall I respond? — Which stretch of time you would normally spend scrolling your phone will you use for meditation today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” (John 7:37). He himself is the source of living water. He also often withdrew to the wilderness to pray (Luke 5:16), drawing strength from the Father. So all his life his leaf never withered, and in due season he bore the fruit of obedience.
lessons.pray: Lord, I want to be that blessed person. Change my appetite so that I delight in your word and meditate on it day and night. Plant me by your streams of water; let my roots go deep, let me bear fruit in season, and let my leaf not wither even in days of drought. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the three voices you spent the most time listening to today
Replace one stretch of phone-scrolling with five minutes meditating on Psalm 1
Draw a tree, and among its roots write a verse you will meditate on
lessons.noon: “But his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” — Lord, right now I sink my roots into your word.

lessons.title: Hiding the Word in My Heart
lessons.theme: Memorizing Scripture means carrying God’s word with you wherever you go

v: How can a young man keep his way pure? By living according to your word.
With my whole heart I have sought you. Don’t let me wander from your commandments.
I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and try to recite this week’s verse, Joshua 1:8, without looking. If you can’t remember part of it, that’s fine—open your Bible, look again, then close your eyes and try once more. Treat this as a walk with the Lord, not an exam.
teach: Money in the bank and cash in your pocket serve different purposes: in an emergency, what you can pull out right away is the money you carry. Scripture is the same. Verses we have read are like savings stored on a bookshelf; verses we have memorized travel with us, ready to be drawn out in the moment of temptation, fear, or when someone needs comfort.

The psalmist asks, “How can a young man keep his way pure?” The answer is “by living according to your word,” and the method is “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” To “hide” here means to treasure something precious. Paul also urges us to let the word of Christ “dwell in you richly,” and then to teach and admonish one another. Memorizing is not only for ourselves; it is also for building others up.

Memorization is not a memory contest; it is letting God’s word become the “mother tongue” of the heart. The method is simple: one verse a week, written on a card, recited together with its reference, three times morning and evening. Don’t worry about going slowly—one verse a week means fifty-two verses living in your heart by the end of the year.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard. A standard that stays only in a book is of no use in a crisis; hidden in the heart, it becomes guidance available at any moment. Memorization is also a practice of humility—admitting that my own thoughts are unreliable and being willing to let God’s words replace mine and reign in my heart.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to entrust his words to you as a treasure. What kind of grace is this?
Who am I? — How many verses are you “carrying with you” in your heart right now?
How shall I respond? — What method will you use this week to memorize Joshua 1:8?
lessons.jesus: At twelve years old, Jesus sat in the temple asking and answering the teachers, and all who heard him were amazed at his understanding (Luke 2:47). Later—in the wilderness, in his preaching, on the cross—Old Testament words were constantly on his lips; even his dying cries came from the Psalms (Psalm 22:1; 31:5). God’s word had long been hidden in his heart.
lessons.pray: Lord, I want to hide your word in my heart so that I might not sin against you. Help me keep up the discipline of memorization—not to impress anyone, but to know you better and obey you more fully. Let the word of Christ dwell in me richly and flow from my lips to bless others. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write Joshua 1:8 on a card and recite it three times morning and evening
Divide this week’s verse into three parts and memorize one more part each day
Share a verse you know by heart with someone who needs it today
lessons.noon: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” — Lord, right now I treasure your word in my heart.

lessons.title: Carrying Scripture Through the Day
lessons.theme: Sitting, walking, lying down and rising up—walking with God’s word

v: These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;
and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
when I remember you on my bed, and think about you in the night watches.

lessons.still: Think ahead to four moments in your day: getting up, going out, eating, and lying down. Quietly pair a short verse with each moment, like setting out four lamps in advance along the path of your day.
teach: People used to tie a knot in a handkerchief to remind themselves not to forget something. God likewise taught Israel to “tie” his words into daily life in all kinds of ways: keeping them on their hearts, teaching them to their children, talking of them whether sitting or walking. Meditation is not just a slot of time in the morning; it is a melody playing in the background of the whole day.

Deuteronomy 6 names four everyday settings: “when you sit in your house,” “when you walk by the way,” “when you lie down,” and “when you rise up”—covering home, going out, rest and new beginnings. God’s word is not meant to be kept in a religious compartment but to seep into every crack of ordinary life. David too says that he remembers God on his bed and thinks about him in the night watches; even sleepless hours became times of meditation.

Here is a practical approach: in the morning, choose one verse; at midday, pray a one-line arrow prayer; in the evening, recall where that verse met you during the day. Little by little, Scripture will surface on its own while you wait at a red light, stand in a queue, or are misunderstood—that is the Holy Spirit reminding you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. Carrying Scripture through the day gives the Spirit “material” to remind us with. Earthly, temporary things often fill our thoughts; Scripture lifts our eyes back to heavenly, eternal things. The focus is on Jesus, not on our circumstances.
q: Who is God? — God wants to be part of your sitting, walking, lying down and rising up. What kind of God is he?
Who am I? — At what time of your day are you most likely to forget God?
How shall I respond? — In which everyday moment today will you set down a verse of Scripture?
lessons.jesus: Jesus often drew his teaching from everyday life: a sower, the birds of the air, the lilies of the field, yeast, a woman searching for a lost coin. In his eyes, ordinary life was the very place to walk with the Father. He taught on the road, at the dinner table, in a boat—God’s word and his life were never separated.
lessons.pray: Lord, I don’t want to remember you only in the morning and then forget you all day. Let your word go with me as I sit, walk, lie down and rise up. When I am busy and scattered, let the Holy Spirit remind me of a verse; when I wake in the night, let me think of you. May my day be filled with your word. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Make this week’s verse your phone’s lock screen
Before each meal, meditate on this week’s verse once before you start eating
Before bed, recall: at what moment today did this verse come to mind?
lessons.noon: “I remember you on my bed, and think about you in the night watches.” — Lord, right now I remember you in the midst of ordinary life.

lessons.title: Meditation Leads to Obedience
lessons.theme: True meditation ends with turning our steps toward God

v: I considered my ways, and turned my steps to your statutes.
I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.
One who has my commandments and keeps them, that person is one who loves me. One who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and will reveal myself to him.”

lessons.still: Recall one verse you meditated on this week and quietly ask, “Lord, what specific action does this verse want me to change?” Wait for a while, then write down whatever comes to your heart.
teach: You can know a recipe by heart, but if you never cook, your family still goes hungry. Meditation that stops at admiration and being moved is like endlessly reading recipes. The order in Joshua 1:8 is clear: meditate day and night “that you may observe to do” it. The end point of meditation is not feeling moved but taking action.

The psalmist says, “I considered my ways, and turned my steps to your statutes.” After considering comes “turning my steps,” and then “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey.” Meditation is like a mirror that shows the gap between my ways and God’s statutes; once I see it, I adjust my steps at once. Jesus also said that the one who has his commandments and keeps them is the one who loves him—and he will reveal himself to that person. Obedience opens the door to knowing the Lord more deeply.

This week we have learned: meditation is chewing the cud → a tree by the streams → hiding the word in our hearts → carrying Scripture through the day → and today, meditation leads to obedience. In the eight steps of changing our mindset, meditation is the bridge from “Revelation” to “Conviction” and “Practice.” Next week we will let this obedience grow into worship and thanksgiving.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your lifestyle. Meditation changes the mindset; obedience changes the life and the lifestyle. Meditation without obedience actually makes us proud—we know more yet still rule ourselves. Only obedient meditation lets Jesus reign.
q: Who is God? — Why does God link “revealing himself” with “keeping his commandments”?
Who am I? — Is there a verse you have read many times but never put into practice?
How shall I respond? — What will you “turn your steps” to do right away today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). For him, God’s word was not only pondered but eaten and lived out. He went from meditation to obedience, all the way to the cross, “becoming obedient to death.”
lessons.pray: Lord, I don’t want to be only a hearer of the word but a doer as well. Let your word light up my path, so that when I see, I turn my steps toward you and hurry to obey without delay. I want to show my love for you by obeying; please reveal yourself to me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: From the verses you meditated on this week, choose one specific action and complete it today
Note one act of obedience you have kept putting off, and take the first step today
Recite Joshua 1:8 to a spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.” — Lord, right now I turn my steps toward you.

mem.t: Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.

lessons.title: Worship Gives God the Glory
lessons.theme: The center of worship is God, not my feelings

v: Ascribe to the LORD the glory due to his name. Worship the LORD in holy array.
But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.

lessons.still: Quietly turn your gaze away from your own needs and think of just one thing: who God is. Slowly name three of his attributes—for example, “You are holy; you are faithful; you are loving”—pausing after each one.
teach: Many people treat worship like a performance: the singers and the preacher are on stage, we are the audience, and on the way out we hand out scores. Were the songs good today? Was I moved? But in true worship God is the audience, and every one of us is an offerer. The question is not “What did I get?” but “What did God receive?”

“Ascribe to Yahweh the glory due to his name.” Worship gives back to God the glory that already belongs to him; it is a kind of “returning.” Jesus told the woman at the well that the Father is seeking those who worship him “in spirit and truth.” “In spirit” means worship flows from a heart renewed by the Holy Spirit, not bound by place or form; “in truth” means coming before God according to the truth, without pretense.

So worship is not only one hour on Sunday; it is the direction of a whole life—turning from self-centeredness to God-centeredness. When we give glory to God we lose nothing; instead we return to the place we were created for. Human beings were made, in the first place, to glorify God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The two cores—let Jesus reign; let Jesus receive all the glory. Self-ruled worship is about our own feelings, and may even steal a little glory for ourselves; self-emptied worship lifts up God alone. Let people be people and let God be God—worship is the most direct declaration of where we belong.
q: Who is God? — Is God worthy of glory because of what he has done for you, or because of who he is?
Who am I? — When you worship, does your focus usually fall on your own feelings or on God?
How shall I respond? — How will you prepare your heart before the next time you worship?
lessons.jesus: The goal of Jesus’ whole life was to glorify the Father. Before his suffering he prayed, “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4). His worship was not confined to the temple; it was in every obedient step he took.
lessons.pray: Holy God, you are worthy of all glory, honor and praise. Forgive me for so often turning worship into my own enjoyment. Today I want to worship you in spirit and truth, giving you the glory due to your name. May my whole life be turned toward you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three attributes of God, and pair each one with a sentence of praise
Arrive five minutes early to your next gathering and quietly prepare your heart
After finishing a task today, pray silently, “This glory belongs to you”
lessons.noon: “Ascribe to the LORD the glory due to his name.” — Lord, right now I give the glory to you.

lessons.title: In Everything Give Thanks
lessons.theme: Thanksgiving is seeing God’s hand in every situation

v: Always rejoice.
Pray without ceasing.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
Praise the LORD, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name!
Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits,

lessons.still: Look back over the last twenty-four hours, slowly, like rewinding a video. Each time you notice a small grace—a cup of hot water, a kind greeting, arriving home safely—pause and softly say, “Thank you, Lord.”
teach: Put on a pair of grey-tinted glasses and the whole world looks dull and overcast; switch to clear lenses and the same street bursts into color. Complaining and thanksgiving are like two pairs of glasses: the circumstances haven’t changed, but the world we see is completely different. To give thanks in everything is to look at life through the lenses of faith.

Paul says, “In everything give thanks”—that is, give thanks in every situation. We don’t thank God for evil or suffering in themselves, but in any circumstance we can see that God still reigns and is still good. This is “the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” David, for his part, speaks to his own soul: “Don’t forget all his benefits.” Thanksgiving needs a good memory; ingratitude usually comes from forgetfulness.

Thanksgiving is a habit we can practise. Write down three things you are thankful for each day, and after a while you will find yourself seeing grace in the very moment things happen. Complaining makes the heart narrower and narrower; thanksgiving makes it wider and wider. Calculating gains and losses with the head brings worry; counting graces with the heart brings joy.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The last step on the path of service is “God”—giving glory to God and giving thanks in everything. Complaining is the voice of the self-ruled life: “Things should go my way.” Thanksgiving is the voice of the self-emptied life: “Lord, you reign, and you are good.” Giving thanks turns our focus away from our circumstances and back to Jesus.
q: Who is God? — In the midst of your recent difficulties, what good things has God still been doing?
Who am I? — Do you more often wear the glasses of complaint or the glasses of thanksgiving?
How shall I respond? — What seemingly ordinary thing will you give thanks for today?
lessons.jesus: Facing five loaves and two fish, Jesus looked up to heaven and blessed them (Mark 6:41). On the night he was betrayed, he took bread and gave thanks (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). He gave thanks when there was not enough, and he gave thanks when suffering was near. His thanksgiving did not depend on favorable circumstances but on trust in his Father.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I often forget your benefits and see only what is lacking or going wrong. Heal my forgetful heart, and let me see your hand in everything. Praise the Lord, my soul! Today I choose thanksgiving instead of complaint, because you are good. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three specific things you are thankful for today
Every time you feel like complaining today, first say one sentence of thanks
Thank someone who has helped you, face to face
lessons.noon: “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” — Lord, right now I give thanks for this moment.

lessons.title: Songs at Midnight
lessons.theme: Praising God in hardship is faith’s loudest declaration

v: But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.

For even though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines, the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls,
yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!

lessons.still: Think of something weighing on you right now. You don’t need to rush to solve it. Before it, softly say, “Lord, even if this hasn’t changed yet, you are still worthy of praise.” Then quietly sing or say a line from a hymn or worship song you know well.
teach: Anyone can sing praise in the daytime; it is praise at midnight that shows faith to be real. Paul and Silas had been beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison, their feet fastened in the stocks, their bodies wounded, their future uncertain. By any normal reckoning this was a time to complain, weep and demand answers—yet at midnight they sang.

Notice the order: they did not praise after the earthquake; they praised while nothing had yet changed. “The prisoners were listening to them”—praise in the darkness became the most powerful witness.
