Habakkuk did the same: the fig tree doesn’t flourish, there is no fruit on the vines, no herd in the stalls—a whole string of “nothing,” and then a single “yet”: “yet I will rejoice in Yahweh.” The praise of faith lives in that “yet.”

Praising in hardship is not pretending it doesn’t hurt; it is declaring who God is in the middle of the pain. Praise moves our focus from the prison walls back to the Lord on his throne. Sometimes God changes the circumstances, as when the prison doors flew open; sometimes he changes us first, so that we are free even inside the cell. Either way, praise sets our hearts free first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The focus is on Jesus, not on our circumstances. A proud heart in hardship interrogates God: “Why me?” A humble heart in hardship praises God: “You are still King.” Praise is a declaration that lets God be God, and a weapon by which the self-emptied life overcomes Satan.
q: Who is God? — At midnight in that prison, what kind of God was he still?
Who am I? — Does your praise often wait until “after the earthquake”?
How shall I respond? — In which “not yet changed” situation will you speak your “yet” today?
lessons.jesus: After the Last Supper, Jesus and his disciples “sang a hymn” and “went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26:30). He knew that Gethsemane and the cross lay ahead, yet he walked toward his suffering with a song. He is the one who sings in the night, and he sings with us at midnight.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often wait for my circumstances to change before I praise you. Today, in the places where I still cannot see a way out, I choose to say, “Yet I will rejoice in you.” Make my praise a witness in the darkness, and loosen the chains in my heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Sing or recite a song of praise over a difficulty that hasn’t been resolved yet
Following Habakkuk 3:17–18, write your own “Though… yet…”
Send a song of praise to a friend who is going through a hard time
lessons.noon: “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!” — Lord, right now I praise you in the midst of hardship.

lessons.title: Life as a Living Sacrifice
lessons.theme: True worship is offering our whole selves

v: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.
Through him, then, let’s offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name.

lessons.still: Offer your body to the Lord from head to toe, one part at a time: “Lord, my mind, my eyes, my mouth, my hands, my feet—they are all yours.” Pause after each one and let that part of you grow still.
teach: In the Old Testament, once a sacrifice was offered it was burned up—a dead sacrifice. New Testament worship is a “living sacrifice”: we are still alive, yet we belong wholly to God. It is like a gift laid on the altar that wakes up each morning still on the altar and does not climb down to take itself back. The hardest thing about a living sacrifice is that it keeps wanting to crawl off the altar.

Paul says, “I urge you… by the mercies of God.” Offering ourselves is a response to grace, not a way of earning it. “Present your bodies” shows that worship includes how we use our bodies: the words we speak, the things we look at, the work of our hands, the paths our feet walk. Such service is our “spiritual service,” the only fitting response. Hebrews adds that the praise of our lips is also a sacrifice—“the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name.”

The key to a living sacrifice is in verse 2: “be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” Change your mindset and you change your life—no longer pressed into the world’s mold, but letting God’s word reshape our thinking. Then Monday’s work at the office, Wednesday’s chores in the kitchen and Friday’s conversation with our children can all become worship.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life keeps life for itself; the self-emptied life offers it to God and enters into the limitless. Shifting from a human perspective to God’s perspective means moving from “This is my body, my time” to “All of this belongs to the Lord.” Letting Jesus reign means staying on the altar day after day.
q: Who is God? — God has first treated you with “mercies.” How does that change your motive for offering yourself?
Who am I? — Which part of your life most often “crawls off the altar”?
How shall I respond? — Which part of your body will you especially offer for the Lord’s use today?
lessons.jesus: Hebrews says that when Christ came into the world, he said to God, “You prepared a body for me” (Hebrews 10:5). With that body Jesus walked, healed, touched lepers, and finally offered it up on the cross. He is the perfect sacrifice, and he lives in us, enabling us to offer ourselves.
lessons.pray: Merciful Father, because of your compassion I offer my body as a living sacrifice. Renew my mind so that I am not conformed to this world. Today let my mouth praise you, my hands serve others, and my feet walk in your ways. When I want to crawl off the altar, remind me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Choose one part of your body (mouth, hands or eyes) and offer it especially to the Lord today
Treat one ordinary task today as worship, offering it to God before you begin
Before bed, offer one sentence of praise as today’s “sacrifice of the lips”
lessons.noon: “To present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God” — Lord, right now I remain on your altar.

lessons.title: Glory to Jesus
lessons.theme: The Lord before whom every knee will bow reigns in my life today

v: Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,
that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth,
and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

lessons.still: Imagine yourself standing in the great worship of heaven, where countless voices lift up the Lamb as one. Gently kneel, or kneel in your heart, and say, “Jesus Christ is Lord.” Let these words be your first declaration today.
teach: In an orchestra, every instrument has its own sound, yet all of them watch the same conductor. If the violin tries to steal the melody or the drummer tries to drown out everyone else, music becomes noise. Worship is the same: we each have different gifts and places, yet we all point to the same One—Jesus Christ.

Philippians 2 moves from Jesus emptying himself (verses 6–8) to God exalting him (verses 9–11): “Therefore God also highly exalted him.” Those in heaven, on earth and under the earth will bow the knee and confess that “Jesus Christ is Lord,” and the end of it all is “to the glory of God the Father.” Paul brings this right down into the most ordinary life: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”

This week we have learned: worship gives God the glory → in everything give thanks → praise in hardship → life as a living sacrifice → and today, glory to Jesus. Next week we will come to know the Holy Spirit, who enables us to worship, to give thanks and to offer ourselves—living from the heart by the Spirit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Our one purpose—building what belongs to God—is the fulfilment of the last line of the Lord’s Prayer: yours is the kingdom, the power and the glory. The self-ruled life quietly keeps a little glory for itself; the self-emptied life gives all the glory to Jesus, and is set free in doing so.
q: Who is God? — From self-emptying to exaltation: what does Jesus’ path show you about the way God works?
Who am I? — In which of your achievements are you still quietly keeping some glory for yourself?
How shall I respond? — In what small matter will you “do all to the glory of God” today?
lessons.jesus: After performing miracles, Jesus often told people not to spread the news; he said, “I don’t seek my own glory” (John 8:50). He gave the glory to the Father, and the Father glorified him. Today the Holy Spirit also glorifies Jesus (John 16:14), and our worship joins in this eternal glory.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are Lord of lords, and every knee will bow before you. Today I kneel before you first and confess that you are my Lord. Whether I eat or drink, or whatever I do, help me do it all to the glory of God. Yours is the kingdom, the power and the glory, forever. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Three times today, declare in your heart, “Jesus Christ is Lord”
When you are praised, quietly turn the glory back to the Lord
Share one thing you are thankful for from this week with a spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “Or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” — Lord, right now all glory belongs to you.

mem.t: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.

lessons.title: The Spirit Dwells in the Heart
lessons.theme: My body is the temple of the Holy Spirit; my heart is his home

v: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them.
Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own,
for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.

lessons.still: Sit quietly and notice your breathing. With each breath in, silently say, “Holy Spirit”; with each breath out, “I am yours.” Continue for a minute, reminding yourself that he is not far away in the sky—he lives within me.
teach: A house where the owner has moved in is completely different from a house that merely has the owner’s photo hanging on the wall. Many Christians know that God is “in heaven” but are not aware that God is “within.” One of the most astonishing announcements of the New Testament is that almighty God, by his Holy Spirit, has come to live in our hearts.

Ezekiel prophesied that God would perform a “heart transplant”: taking away the heart of stone, giving a heart of flesh, and “I will put my Spirit within you.” This promise was fulfilled after Pentecost. That is why Paul says, “Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.” In the Old Testament, God’s presence dwelt in the temple; in the New Testament, God dwells in believers. The result: “You are not your own,” for we “were bought with a price.”

The Spirit dwells in the heart, not in the head. This is not opposition to thinking; it means that the center of the spiritual life is the heart—the seat of will, emotion and trust. We do not strain with our minds to figure God out; we respond in our hearts to the God who has already moved in. Here is the mindset change: God is not merely someone I study but the Master who lives with me.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One of the three foundations—the Holy Spirit is my guide. Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself; living from the heart brings joy, living from the head brings worry. “You are not your own” is the very foundation of the self-emptied life: I belong to the One who lives within me.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to live in your heart. What does this say about how close he longs to be to you?
Who am I? — Are you more often aware of God “in heaven” or God “within”?
How shall I respond? — How will you glorify the Holy Spirit who lives in you with your body today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was baptized, the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form like a dove (Luke 3:22). He was full of the Spirit, was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, and returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit (Luke 4:1, 14). Jesus lived a life indwelt and guided by the Spirit, and he promised to give that same Spirit to us.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for living in me and making my body your temple. I am not my own; I was bought with a price. Be Lord in my heart, take away its hardness, and make me willing to follow your guidance. Today I will glorify God in my body. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Three times today, stop and silently say, “Holy Spirit, you are here”
Choose one bodily habit (eating, sleep, what you look at) and adjust it today for the sake of the Spirit’s temple
Write down one area where “I am not my own” needs to become real
lessons.noon: “Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you” — Lord, right now I acknowledge that you live in me.

lessons.title: The Work of the Counselor
lessons.theme: The Holy Spirit is the One beside us who accompanies, teaches and reminds

v: the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive, for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you and will be in you.
But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.

lessons.still: Quietly ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of something Jesus said. Don’t rush to look it up; simply wait. If a saying comes to mind, repeat it slowly a few times and thank the Spirit for the reminder.
teach: When someone arrives in an unfamiliar city, if a local friend stays by their side the whole time—showing the way, translating, warning them what not to do—they are no longer a lonely traveler. When Jesus was about to leave his disciples, he did not hand them a manual and walk away. He promised that the Father would give them “another Counselor” to be with them forever.

The word translated “Counselor” means “one called alongside”—a comforter, a helper, an advocate. “Another” means one of the same kind as Jesus: the Holy Spirit is not a force but a personal God. His work includes: he “lives with you,” he “will be in you,” he “will teach you all things,” and he “will remind you of all that I said to you.”

So the Spirit’s work cannot be separated from the words of Jesus. What he reminds us of is what Jesus said; where he leads will never contradict Scripture. The more we hide the word in our hearts, the more “material” the Spirit has to remind us with. Scripture is the standard and the Spirit is the guide; when the two work together, we will not veer to the left or to the right.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The three foundations are bound together—Jesus is my example; Scripture is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Spirit always points to Jesus and reminds us of his words. Any “prompting” that exalts the self rather than Jesus needs to be tested by Scripture.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit is “another Counselor.” What is his relationship to Jesus?
Who am I? — Do you often feel like a lonely traveler, forgetting that someone has been beside you all along?
How shall I respond? — How will you pay attention today to the words of Jesus the Spirit brings to mind?
lessons.jesus: While on earth, Jesus personally accompanied, taught and reminded his disciples. Yet he said, “It is to your advantage that I go away” (John 16:7). For after he left, the Holy Spirit could live in every believer, no longer limited by time or place. The presence of the Counselor is the continuation of the presence of Jesus.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, our Counselor, thank you for always being with me and living in me. Teach me to understand the truth, and remind me of Jesus’ words when I need them. When I am lonely, confused or weak, let me remember that you are right beside me. I want to learn to hear your voice. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before reading Scripture, pray, “Holy Spirit, please teach me”
When a verse comes to mind today, write it down and review it in the evening
Send a word of greeting to someone who is lonely, as an instrument of the Spirit’s comfort
lessons.noon: “Will teach you all things” — Lord, right now let your Spirit remind me of your words.

lessons.title: Walking by the Spirit
lessons.theme: Keeping in step with the Spirit naturally bears the fruit of life

v: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.
For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.

lessons.still: Imagine walking side by side with a friend, matching your pace to his—not rushing ahead, not lagging behind. Quietly say to the Holy Spirit, “Today I want to keep in step with you.” Then notice which matter in your heart wants to rush ahead.
teach: In a three-legged race, the key to winning is not who runs fastest but who stays in step. If one person charges off at their own pace, both fall over. When Paul says, “let’s also walk by the Spirit” (verse 25), the word he uses means to fall into line, to march in step—not an occasional sprint, but everyday keeping pace.

Galatians 5 describes a tug-of-war inside us: “the flesh lusts against the Spirit.” The answer is not to clamp down on the flesh by sheer willpower but to “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh”—bring in the light and the darkness retreats on its own. The result is “the fruit of the Spirit.” Notice it is “fruit,” singular: nine qualities like one cluster of grapes, all coming from a single life.

Fruit is not manufactured; it grows. A fruit tree doesn’t have to grit its teeth to produce fruit; it only needs to stay connected to its source of life. If we want love, joy and peace, we don’t “produce” them; we follow the Spirit day by day and let his life flow out naturally. This is the “9” of 920—bearing the ninefold fruit in front of every “2.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The practice of 920—every person in my life is my “2”; I practise the “0” of the self-emptied life; and the “9” is the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Those who have crucified the flesh no longer rule themselves but let the Spirit be Lord, and the fruit grows naturally.
q: Who is God? — The fruit of the Spirit is God’s own character. What does it show you about who he is?
Who am I? — Of the nine fruits, which one is most lacking in your life?
How shall I respond? — With which of your “2”s today will you especially follow the Spirit?
lessons.jesus: The ninefold fruit of the Spirit is a portrait of Jesus: love for sinners, joy in the Father, peace in the storm, patience with his disciples, kindness to children, goodness to the oppressed, faithfulness to the Father, gentleness toward people, and self-control in temptation. Bearing fruit means living out Jesus.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, I often charge ahead at my own pace, and I fall and get hurt. Today I want to walk by you and keep in step with you. Grow in me love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control—especially the one I lack the most. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Choose the fruit you most lack and deliberately practise it toward one person today
When emotions rise, pause for three seconds and ask, “Holy Spirit, how do you want me to respond?”
Before bed, list the nine fruits and tick the ones you experienced today
lessons.noon: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” — Lord, right now I keep in step with you.

lessons.title: Do Not Quench the Spirit
lessons.theme: Be sensitive and responsive to the Spirit; don’t let the fire in your heart go out

v: Don’t quench the Spirit.
Don’t despise prophecies.
Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

lessons.still: Think back to the last time you felt a gentle nudge in your heart—to check on someone, to take back a word, to help with a need. Did you respond? Quietly tell the Lord, “I want to listen and obey you more sensitively.”
teach: A brazier of coals, stirred now and then and fed with fresh charcoal, burns brighter and brighter; douse it with cold water or leave it alone, and soon only ashes remain. When Paul says, “Don’t quench the Spirit,” “quench” means to put out a fire. The Holy Spirit often gives gentle promptings in our hearts; ignore them again and again, and the heart slowly grows cold.

In the same passage Paul gives balance. On one hand, “Don’t quench” and “Don’t despise”; on the other, “Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.” Not every thought is from the Spirit, so we must test; but neither should we ignore everything for fear of getting it wrong. Ephesians uses relational language: “Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God.” The Spirit is a person, and he is grieved by our bitterness, anger and lies.

How can we discern the Spirit’s prompting? It agrees with Scripture, exalts Jesus, and makes us more humble and more loving. It is usually a quiet, clear nudge that brings peace, not panic and condemnation. The best training is “prompt obedience in small things”: if he prompts you to make a phone call, make it; if he prompts you to keep quiet, keep quiet.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled person evaluates with the head: “Is this worth it? Will I lose face?”—and so douses the prompting. The self-emptied person responds from the heart to the Spirit and lets him be Lord. Scripture is the standard and the Spirit is the guide: test by Scripture, respond with obedience, and the fire burns ever brighter.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit can be “grieved.” What does this show you about how close his relationship with you is?
Who am I? — Is there a recent prompting that you put out with reasons and excuses?
How shall I respond? — If a small nudge comes today, are you willing to obey right away?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). He was exquisitely sensitive to the Father’s heart: waiting by a well for one woman, stopping in a jostling crowd to ask who had touched him. He never let busyness quench the Father’s promptings.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, forgive me for the many times I have doused your promptings with excuses, and for grieving you with bitterness and anger. Kindle the fire in my heart again. Give me wisdom to discern and courage to obey, so that I respond to you at once in small things. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: When you sense a prompting to do good today, act on it within ten minutes
Write down a recent prompting you ignored, confess it to the Lord, and make it right
Before you speak, ask: “Would these words grieve the Holy Spirit?”
lessons.noon: “Don’t quench the Spirit.” — Lord, right now I want to respond to your gentle voice.

lessons.title: Guard Your Heart
lessons.theme: Life flows from the heart; a Spirit-filled heart is a wellspring

v: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.
that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love,

lessons.still: Imagine that your heart is a well. Quietly ask the Lord to clear away the debris at its mouth—a worry, a grudge, a craving—taking them out one by one and handing them to him. Then ask the Holy Spirit to rise up like living water from the bottom of the well.
teach: If a river is polluted upstream, the cities downstream will struggle no matter how much they filter; protecting the source is the most fundamental way to protect the whole city. Many people put great effort into managing their words, behavior and image (downstream) but give little care to their own hearts (upstream).

Proverbs says, “Keep your heart with all diligence,” because “out of it is the wellspring of life.” Our words, choices, relationships and ministry all flow from this source. Paul’s prayer for the Ephesians was also about the heart: “that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith.” The Spirit works from the inside out.

This week we have seen: the Spirit dwells in the heart → the Counselor accompanies and teaches → walking by the Spirit → not quenching the Spirit → and today, guarding this heart in which the Spirit lives. A heart ruled by the Spirit naturally pours out self-giving love. Next week we will learn Jesus’ way of self-denial: living for Jesus and for others.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life flows from the heart—live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself. Transformation begins in the heart: when the heart changes, lifestyle, relationships and ministry change with it. Life first, then relationships, then ministry; guarding the heart is guarding the source of all of these.
q: Who is God? — Why does God care most about your heart rather than your outward performance?
Who am I? — What is polluting your “upstream” right now?
How shall I respond? — How will you guard your heart today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). He rebuked the Pharisees for cleaning the outside of the cup and plate while inside they were full of extortion and self-indulgence (Matthew 23:25). Jesus always cares about the heart, because he renews a person from the heart outward.
lessons.pray: Lord, search my heart and remove the pollution within. I want to guard my heart above all else. Strengthen me with power through your Spirit in my inner being, so that Christ may dwell in my heart through faith. May my words, choices and relationships all flow from a heart filled with you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Review three kinds of information that entered your heart today, and cut out one that does not build you up
Before starting each task, silently pray, “Lord, guard my heart”
Share with a spiritual companion one reminder the Holy Spirit gave you this week
lessons.noon: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” — Lord, right now I give my heart to you to guard.

mem.t: For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.title: The Son of Man Came to Serve
lessons.theme: Jesus redefines greatness: whoever wants to be great must be a servant

v: Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.still: Quietly picture Jesus kneeling down to serve you. Then ask yourself, “Today, do I want to be served, or do I want to serve?” Don’t rush to answer; just let the question rest in your heart for a while.
teach: The world is a pyramid: the higher you climb, the fewer people there are, and the more people serve you. Jesus’ kingdom is an upside-down pyramid: the higher you go, the more people you carry. When James and John asked to sit at Jesus’ right and left, they were imagining God’s kingdom as the world’s pyramid.

Jesus first describes the world’s pattern: rulers “lord it over them,” great ones “exercise authority over them”—power pressing downward. Then he says, “But it shall not be so among you.” In God’s kingdom, “whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant,” and “whoever… wants to become first among you, shall be bondservant of all.” Then he points to himself: the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life. Jesus did not merely teach self-denial; he himself is self-denial.

This doesn’t mean losing our sense of worth or letting people walk all over us. It means choosing freely to serve from a secure identity. Precisely because we know who we are, we don’t need others to serve us in order to prove ourselves. Here is the mindset shift: greatness is not how many people work for me, but how many people I lay down my life for.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride grasps power and demands to be served; humility lays down power and serves others. Service on the path of service means letting Jesus reign and serving under his authority, not building a kingdom of our own. The upside-down pyramid is the shape of what belongs to God.
q: Who is God? — The King of kings “came to serve.” What does this show you about God’s heart?
Who am I? — At home or at church, do you more often expect to be served or take the initiative to serve?
How shall I respond? — In what concrete way will you “be a servant” today?
lessons.jesus: Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, Jesus rose, wrapped a towel around his waist, and washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:3–5). He did not serve because he lacked status; it was because he was so sure of his status that he could kneel so freely. His highest service was laying down his life on the cross as a ransom for many.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you came not to be served but to serve, and to give your life for me. Tear down the pride in my heart that wants to climb to the top of the pyramid. Today I want to be a servant—at home, at work and in the church. May you receive the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Take on a household chore today that someone else usually does
In a meeting or gathering, listen to others first and speak last
Write down where you most want to be served, and give it over to the Lord
lessons.noon: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve” — Lord, right now I want to serve as you did.

lessons.title: A Grain of Wheat
lessons.theme: Self-denial is not loss but the gaining of a richer life

v: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.
However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.

Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ

lessons.still: Hold something you treasure (or imagine holding it), then slowly open your hand. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I let go, because you are more precious than all of this.” Notice what you feel in your heart as you let go.
teach: If a farmer cannot bear to plant his seed and keeps it in the barn for years, it remains a single seed. But once it is buried in the soil and seemingly lost, at harvest time it becomes a whole field of wheat. Human eyes see “loss”; God’s eyes see “harvest.”

When Jesus spoke these words, he was facing the cross: if a grain of wheat dies, “it bears much fruit.” Then he widened the principle to every disciple: “He who loves his life will lose it.” Paul experienced this principle firsthand. The credentials he once took pride in he now counted “as a loss,” even “nothing but refuse,” because he had gained a far greater treasure—“the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord.”

The secret of self-denial is not grimly giving things up but seeing something better. A child won’t let go of the sweet in his hand until he sees the better gift in his father’s hand. The self-emptied life is not emptiness; it is entering the limitless—letting go of a limited self to gain the limitless Christ. This is the mystery and the joy of self-denial.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life is not losing yourself; it is letting the limited “me” enter the limitless Christ. The shift in perspective is from the temporary to the eternal, from the earthly to the heavenly. The self-ruled person clutches a single grain of wheat; the self-emptied person is willing to fall into the ground and bear much fruit.
q: Who is God? — God works through “dying and bearing fruit.” What does this show you about his wisdom?
Who am I? — What are you clutching tightly that you can’t bear to “plant”?
How shall I respond? — What will you be willing to “count as loss” and hand over to the Lord today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is that grain of wheat. He fell into the ground and died, rose on the third day, and has borne fruit in countless lives across the generations—including yours and mine. Not one bit of the life he laid down was wasted; instead it became life for all.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died for me so that I might live. Give me eyes to see that self-denial is not loss but harvest. I hand over to you what I have been clutching, because knowing you is the greatest treasure. Let my life, too, bear much fruit. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: List the three things you find hardest to let go of, and pray to the Lord about each one
Today, give up a small right—a seat, the conversation, the choice—to someone else
Copy out Philippians 3:8 and tuck it into your wallet or phone case
lessons.noon: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone.” — Lord, right now I am willing to fall into the ground.

lessons.title: For Others, Not for Myself
lessons.theme: Self-denial means turning our eyes from ourselves to others

v: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.

lessons.still: Think of someone you will meet today, and pray one line for them in your heart: “Lord, bless them.” Then ask, “What might they need today?” Wait quietly and let the Holy Spirit give you a concrete idea.
teach: After a group photo is taken and lands on everyone’s phone, who do most of us look for first? Ourselves. We naturally put ourselves at the center of the picture. The practice of self-denial is learning, in every snapshot of life, to see others first.

Paul gives three concrete turns: “doing nothing through rivalry” (no little cliques of our own), “or through conceit” (no grabbing the spotlight), and “in humility, each counting others better than himself.” Verse 4 is well balanced: “not just looking to his own things, but… also to the things of others.” It doesn’t say ignore yourself entirely, only not “just” yourself. The motivation comes from the cross: Christ died for all, “that those who live should no longer live to themselves.”

Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. This is not making idols of other people; it is loving those Jesus loves because we love him. The practical question is: “How will this benefit others?” When that becomes a question we ask naturally in our decisions, the self-centered “self” gradually steps aside.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The practice of 920—every person in my life is my “2,” and before them I live out the “0” of the self-emptied life. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; when I first count others better than myself, humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
q: Who is God? — Christ “died for all.” How does he see every person?
Who am I? — In the “group photo” of your life, who do you usually look for first?
How shall I respond? — Whose concerns will you especially “look to” today?
lessons.jesus: On the cross, in agonizing pain, Jesus still asked the Father to forgive those who crucified him, still entrusted his mother to his disciple, and still promised the repentant thief that he would be with him in Paradise (Luke 23:34, 43; John 19:26–27). In his moment of greatest suffering, his eyes were still on others.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you died for me so that I would no longer live for myself. Turn my eyes away from myself to see the needs of those around me. Give me a humble heart that counts others better than myself, and a love that looks to the interests of others. I want to live for you and for others. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In conversations today, ask how the other person is doing first; listen more and talk less about yourself
Quietly finish something a colleague or family member needs done
Before making a decision, ask: “How will this benefit others?”
lessons.noon: “Each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” — Lord, right now help me see the people around me.

lessons.title: People Matter More Than Tasks
lessons.theme: Don’t hurt people for the sake of tasks, and don’t overlook people for the sake of tasks

v: By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.

lessons.still: Think through today’s to-do list, then quietly ask the Lord, “Is there anyone today I ‘passed by on the other side’ because I was busy with tasks?” Let that person’s face come to mind, and pray for them.
teach: A mother rushes to get the house spotless before guests arrive, and snaps impatiently at the child trailing at her heels. The floor shines, but the child’s heart darkens. Scenes like this play out in many homes and many churches: the task gets done, but people get hurt.

The priest and the Levite were both religious workers. They “saw” the wounded man but “passed by on the other side”—perhaps hurrying to their duties, perhaps afraid of becoming unclean. The Samaritan also “saw,” but he “was moved with compassion,” interrupted his own journey, and gave oil, wine, his animal, his time and his money. The lawyer asked, “Who is my neighbor?” but Jesus turned the question around: “Which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” The focus moves from definition to action.

People matter more than tasks, because people have eternal value and tasks are temporary. This doesn’t mean tasks are unimportant; it means tasks exist for the sake of people. When a church wounds its co-workers for the sake of an event, or a family sacrifices relationships for the sake of grades, things are upside down. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—when the order is right, ministry will be blessed.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; don’t hurt people for the sake of tasks. The order of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, then with tasks. The priest put the “task” ahead of the “person”; the Samaritan put the person back where he belonged.
q: Who is God? — In telling this parable, what does Jesus show you that God values?
Who am I? — Have you recently “passed by” someone because you were rushing to get things done?
How shall I respond? — For whom will you stop what you are doing today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was hurrying to heal Jairus’ dying daughter, yet on the way he stopped to ask who had touched him, until the woman with the flow of blood told him the whole truth (Mark 5:30–34). In his eyes, this overlooked woman mattered just as much as the synagogue ruler’s daughter. He never neglected people because a task was urgent.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that in trying to do things well I often hurt the people around me, and in rushing to keep my schedule I pass by those in need. Give me the eyes and the heart of the Samaritan, to be moved with compassion when I see, and to be willing to stop. Teach me to live as though people matter more than tasks. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Put down your phone or your work for someone today and give them ten minutes of full attention
Offer an apology or a word of care to someone you have neglected because of tasks
Look over this week’s calendar and set aside time for a relationship
lessons.noon: “When he saw him, he was moved with compassion.” — Lord, right now let me stop for people.

lessons.title: Relationships Matter More Than Things
lessons.theme: Possessions will pass away; love and relationships last forever

v: He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

lessons.still: Look around at the things near you and quietly ask, “Is there anything here that occupies my heart more than people do?” Then think of three people you love, and thank the Lord for each of them in a sentence.
teach: After a house fire, the owner standing in the ashes doesn’t first ask, “Is my TV still there?” but “Is my family safe?” In a crisis we know exactly what matters; yet on ordinary days we often quarrel over things and damage our peace over money.

Jesus said, “A man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.” Zacchaeus had exploited his own people for money and cut himself off from them. After meeting Jesus, his very first response was to deal with money and relationships: “half of my goods I give to the poor,” and “if I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.” When Jesus came into his house, money went from being his master to being his tool—used to repair relationships. True salvation changes our relationship with both things and people.

This week we have learned: the Son of Man came to serve → a grain of wheat → for others, not for myself → people matter more than tasks → relationships matter more than things. This is also the final theme of Stage One, “Rooting.” Next week is a retreat week: we will pause to look back on what God has done over these twelve weeks, count his graces, and prepare to enter “Growing.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The fivefold change—mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships, ministry. Once Zacchaeus’s mindset changed, his life, lifestyle and relationships followed. Relationships matter more than things, because people are loved by God and things are only tools for serving people. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him be Lord of my wallet.
q: Who is God? — Jesus took the initiative to “seek” Zacchaeus. What does this show you about how much God values people?
Who am I? — Have you recently damaged a relationship over things or money?
How shall I respond? — What could you use today to bless or repair which relationship?
lessons.jesus: On earth Jesus had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58), yet his life was full of relationships: disciples, tax collectors, sinners, women, children. He used the most precious thing he had—his own life—to redeem us, reconciling us to God and to one another.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you gave up everything to seek me. Help me see clearly that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. Set me free from greed, and teach me to use what is in my hands to bless people and repair relationships. May my relationship with you and with others be more precious than anything I own. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Use a small sum of money or an item to bless someone in need
Take the first step toward reconciliation over a dispute about things or money
Prepare for next week’s retreat: write down the one thing you are most thankful for from these twelve weeks
lessons.noon: “For a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.” — Lord, right now I choose to treasure people more than things.

mem.t: I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

lessons.title: A Change of Mindset
lessons.theme: Looking back over twelve weeks at how God has renewed my mind

v: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit,
and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind,
and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.

lessons.still: Find a quiet place and give yourself a little more time than usual. Open your notes from these twelve weeks, or simply recall the road you have traveled. Don’t rush to evaluate; just quietly say to the Lord, “Lord, take me back to see the footprints you have walked with me.”
teach: Climbers halfway up a mountain will sit down on a big rock and look back. Looking up, the summit is still far away; looking down, they discover how far they have already come. A retreat week is that rock. Stopping is not laziness; it is a chance to see clearly where we have come from, sort out our gear, and then keep climbing.

Paul describes sanctification in three movements: “put away” the old self, “be renewed in the spirit of your mind,” and “put on” the new self. The middle step is the key—renewal of the mind is a change of mindset. Over these twelve weeks we have experienced a whole series of shifts in perspective: from performance to grace (coming home), from busyness to stillness, from piling up knowledge to meeting God (reading Scripture), from my kingdom to your kingdom (prayer), from grasping power to returning to our place (humility and victory).

And more: from anxiety to rest, from feelings to assurance, from speed-reading to meditation, from complaint to thanksgiving, from living from the head by ourselves to living from the heart by the Spirit, from living for ourselves to living for others. Change your mindset and you change your life. Today, pick out the shift that has gone deepest for you and write: “I used to think…, but now I know….”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps of changing our mindset—Information, Revelation, Conviction, Practice, Review, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. A retreat is the time for “Review” and “Correction.” Shifting from a human perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, is a lifelong lesson—and we have already begun.
q: Who is God? — Looking back over twelve weeks, how has God renewed your mindset?
Who am I? — Which old way of thinking is the most stubborn, still tugging at you today?
How shall I respond? — Which new way of thinking will you carry into the next stage?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus walked with two disciples on the road to Emmaus, and “beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Their understanding was renewed by the Lord, their hearts burned within them, and they got up at once to return to Jerusalem. Jesus is glad to walk with us as we look back, helping us understand afresh the road we have traveled.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with me these twelve weeks. You have renewed so many of my mistaken ideas and shown me your grace and truth. Keep renewing me in the spirit of my mind, so that I put off the old self and put on the new self, created in your likeness. I want to be renewed by you all my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write three sentences beginning “I used to think…, but now I know…”
Review the memory verses from the past twelve weeks and see how many you still remember
Tell a spiritual companion about the deepest change of mindset you have experienced
lessons.noon: “And that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind” — Lord, right now keep renewing my heart.

lessons.title: A Change of Life
lessons.theme: When we remain in the Lord, our lives change naturally and bear fruit

v: Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.
I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.

lessons.still: Clench both hands into fists, a picture of gripping tightly in your own strength. Then slowly relax them and turn your palms upward, a picture of a branch simply joined to the vine. Quietly meditate on this week’s verse: “I am the vine. You are the branches.”
teach: A photograph captures a single moment, but growth only shows up in time-lapse. Looking at yourself day by day, nothing seems to change. But set yourself from twelve weeks ago beside yourself today, and you may notice: a little less temper, a little more prayer, a little more patience with your family.

Jesus says the branch’s secret to bearing fruit is just one thing: “Remain in me.” Not straining to squeeze out fruit, but staying connected. Paul also says that as we see “the glory of the Lord,” we “are transformed into the same image from glory to glory.” Change comes by beholding, not by striving. And it comes “from the Lord, the Spirit”: life change is the work of the Holy Spirit; our part is to remain in the Lord and fix our eyes on him.

So when you look back on how your life has changed, don’t only ask whether you have done well. Ask instead: over these twelve weeks, has my connection with the Lord grown closer? Stillness, Scripture, prayer, meditation, worship—these practices are not the fruit itself; they are the ways a branch stays joined to the vine. Get the connection right, and the fruit will come naturally.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “Apart from me you can do nothing”—this is the declaration of the self-emptied life. The self-ruled person tries to bear fruit by his own effort and grows ever drier; the self-emptied person remains in the Lord, lets Christ live within, and enters the limitless. Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your lifestyle.
q: Who is God? — What does the picture of the vine and the branches show you about God’s relationship with you?
Who am I? — Compared with twelve weeks ago, where do you see change in your life?
How shall I respond? — In the next stage, which practice will you use to keep “remaining in the Lord”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself; but the Father who lives in me does his works” (John 14:10). All his life he bore fruit in connection with the Father. He wants us to remain in him, just as he remains in the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the vine and I am a branch. Thank you for the changes you have made in me over these twelve weeks—small, but real. Apart from you I can do nothing. Help me remain in you, fix my eyes on your glory, and be transformed by you from glory to glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three changes you have seen in your life over these twelve weeks
Ask a family member or friend, “Have you noticed anything different about me these past three months?”
Memorize this week’s verse: John 15:5
lessons.noon: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” — Lord, right now I remain in you.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Stone: A Record of Grace
lessons.theme: Counting God’s graces and raising an Ebenezer to his faithfulness

v: Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.”
It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

lessons.still: Quietly recall one specific way God helped you during these twelve weeks—an answered prayer, a timely comfort, a restored relationship. Treat it like a stone and gently set it down in your heart, saying, “Until now you have helped me.”
teach: Many families mark their children’s height on a doorframe, one line each year. When the children grow up and look back at those lines, they see the story of how they were raised. Our spiritual lives need “height marks” too—recording God’s grace so that in hard times we don’t forget how he once led us.

At Mizpah the Israelites repented and returned to God. When the Philistines came to attack, God thundered with a great voice and threw the enemy into confusion. Samuel then set up a stone and named it “Ebenezer,” meaning “stone of help,” saying, “Yahweh helped us until now.” This stone was both a look back (until now) and an act of faith (God will keep on helping). Jeremiah, too, amid the ruins of the city, remembered that God’s loving kindnesses “are new every morning.”

A record of grace is not boasting about our achievements; it is a testimony to God’s faithfulness. Today, write a list of the graces of these twelve weeks: prayers answered, mindsets renewed, relationships restored, days kept safe. This list will become fuel for the next stretch of the journey, and material for sharing your testimony with others in the future.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The final stop on the path of service is “God”—giving glory to God and giving thanks in everything. A record of grace helps us see that everything has been accomplished by God in Jesus, so the glory does not go to me but to Jesus. Counting God’s graces is a concrete way of letting Jesus receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — “They are new every morning.” How have you experienced God’s faithfulness these twelve weeks?
Who am I? — Do you tend to remember grace, or to forget it?
How shall I respond? — What kind of “Ebenezer” will you set up for these twelve weeks?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus instituted the Lord’s Supper, he said, “Do this in memory of me” (Luke 22:19). He knew how forgetful we are, so he gave us a sign we could repeat again and again. Every time we take Communion, we set up another Ebenezer beneath the cross.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, until now you have helped me. Thank you for the new mercies of every morning these twelve weeks, for holding me up when I was weak and finding me when I was lost. I will remember your deeds and not forget your benefits. May this record be the beginning of a lifelong testimony to your faithfulness. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write a list of at least ten graces from these twelve weeks
Find a small stone or a card and write on it “Ebenezer” and today’s date
Share one grace from your list with a spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “The LORD helped us until now.” — Lord, right now I remember your faithfulness.

lessons.title: Stage Self-Review
lessons.theme: Examining ourselves honestly before the Lord to see the next step clearly

v: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.
Examine your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves. Or don’t you know about your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you?— unless indeed you are disqualified.

lessons.still: Before you begin the self-review, be still for a minute. Tell the Lord, “I am not doing this to give myself a score, or to condemn myself. I only want to see myself clearly in your light.” Let your heart settle, then answer honestly.
teach: After a certain number of miles, a car goes back to the garage for a service: the tyres are checked, the oil is changed, the steering is realigned. This is not because the car is broken but so that it can go further. The spiritual health self-review is the same—not an exam, but regular maintenance to see what has worn down and what needs adjusting.

David prayed, “Search me, God, and know my heart.” The best self-review is not looking in a mirror ourselves but asking God to shine his light, because the human heart is deceitful above all things and we need his light. Paul also urges believers to “examine your own selves” and “test your own selves,” and the focus of that examination is: “Don’t you know… that Jesus Christ is in you?” The heart of the self-review is not a grade but our relationship with Christ.

Face each question honestly: stillness, Scripture, prayer, humility, rest, meditation, worship, following the Spirit, self-denial—which have taken root, and which are still shallow? If your score is high, don’t be proud; if it is low, don’t be discouraged. Once you see clearly, choose one or two areas you most need and carry them into the next stage. This is “Review” and “Correction,” followed by “Repetition.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is the key to revival. The proud don’t want to be searched, afraid of seeing their shortcomings; the humble are willing to return to their place, letting God be God and people be people—admitting they need to grow. The purpose of the self-review is to let Jesus reign in more areas of our lives.
q: Who is God? — When God searches us, is it to condemn us, or to “lead me in the everlasting way”?
Who am I? — Among these practices, which is your strongest? Which is your weakest?
How shall I respond? — In the next stage, which one or two practices will you prioritize strengthening?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). This was the gentlest and also the deepest examination. The Lord was not trying to humiliate him but to restore him. When we review ourselves before the Lord, the core question he asks is always the same: Do you love me?
lessons.pray: God, search me and know my heart; try me and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way. I am not afraid to be honest before you, because you are the Father who loves me. Show me where I need to grow stronger in the next step. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Complete this stage's spiritual health self-review
From the results of your self-review, circle the one practice that most needs strengthening
Share your self-review results with a spiritual parent or companion and ask them to pray for you
lessons.noon: “Search me, God, and know my heart.” — Lord, right now I open myself in your light.

lessons.title: Resolving to Enter Growing
lessons.theme: Deep roots make tall growth; forgetting what is behind, stretching forward to what is ahead

v: As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,
rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Quietly stand up (or stand up in your heart) and face forward. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I have begun to put down roots; now I want to move forward with you.” Take one area in which you want to grow and receive it from the Lord’s hand, like a runner taking the baton.
teach: Some kinds of bamboo show little sign of life above ground for the first few years after planting, because they are spreading their roots underground. Once the roots are established, the speed of their upward growth is astonishing. These thirteen weeks of “Rooting” may not have been dramatic, but they have laid the foundation for the “Growing” to come.

Paul uses two pictures for Christian growth. First, “rooted and built up in him”—like a tree putting down roots, like a house laid on its foundation. Then, “forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal”—like a race. We put down roots in order to run, and we run by drawing on our roots. “Forgetting what is behind” means neither being bound by past failures nor resting on past achievements; “stretching forward” aims at “the prize of the high calling of God.”

This brings Stage One, “Rooting,” to a close. We came home; we learned stillness, Scripture reading, prayer, humility, victory and rest; we gained assurance; we learned meditation, worship, dependence on the Spirit and self-denial. In the next stage, “Growing,” we will set out from our identity in Christ and let branches and leaves grow from these roots. Write down one sentence of resolve, and with a thankful heart, press on toward the goal.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Stage One put down roots in our relationship with God; the growth ahead will extend this life to ourselves, to others and to our tasks. Our one purpose: to build what belongs to God. We do not grow for our own sake, but so that Jesus may reign and receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — The God who calls you “from above”—what are his intentions for your next stage?
Who am I? — What lies behind you that you need to “forget”—the chains of failure, or past achievements?
How shall I respond? — Write one sentence of resolve as you enter the “Growing” stage.
lessons.jesus: Scripture records that “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:52). He spent many ordinary years in Nazareth before stepping out into public ministry. His growth was whole and steady; and today he lives in us, leading us step by step to grow up into maturity.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for bringing me through these thirteen weeks of rooting. I will forget what is behind, stretch forward to what is ahead, and press on toward the goal. Make me rooted and built up in you, established in the faith, and abounding in thanksgiving. Lead me into the season of growing; may you reign, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write a sentence of resolve and put it up where you have your daily devotions
Choose two practices to continue in the next stage, and set a regular time for each
Invite a spiritual companion to commit with you to praying for each other through the next stage
lessons.noon: “Forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before” — Lord, right now I move forward with you.
